page_title: 'It's really hard to believe' - How Oregon primary school shooting unfolded - BBC News
summary: Three children aged 5, 8 and 11 and a teacher were killed after a 16-year-old suspect opened fire in the city of Bend, local police say.
text: 'It's really hard to believe' - How Oregon primary school shooting unfolded 'It's really hard to believe' - How Oregon primary school shooting unfolded Close Four victims, including a teacher and three children aged 5, 8 and 11, were killed in a shooting at a primary school in the US state of Oregon, local police say. A 16-year-old suspect forced his way into the school by firing at locked doors. He was also killed in the shooting by an armed member of the community who followed the suspect inside the school, police said at a press conference. Two additional victims, a 7-year-old and another teacher, were hurt and transported to hospital in critical condition. title: Actor Imran Khan ordered to leave India after participating in protest
page_title: Imran Khan: Bollywood actor asked to leave India after participating in CJP protest in Mumbai - BBC News
summary: The Bollywood actor had been detained and released while participating in a protest in Mumbai on 10 October.
text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Imran Khan had been briefly detained by the police on 10 October while participating in a protest in Mumbai By Meryl Sebastian BBC News Published 15 October 2026 Authorities in India have ordered actor Imran Khan, nephew of Bollywood star Aamir Khan, to leave the country by 28 October after he participated in a protest, seeking electoral reforms. An American citizen, Khan holds an Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) card, which allows people of Indian origin to visit and stay in the country. But an OCI cannot vote or contest elections. "Imran Khan participated in the agitation at Mumbai's August Kranti Maidan, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar," police said in a statement on Thursday. Khan's lawyer has said the actor will challenge the order in the Bombay High Court. Police said the Foreigners' Regional Registration Office (FRRO) had served Khan a notice for violating laws by protesting. But the actor's lawyer said that no provision of the law or any rule for OCI cardholders prohibit him from participating in a protest. The Press Trust of India reports that the actor's petition against the Mumbai police notice termed it as "drastic". Khan is known for the 2008 hit romantic comedy Jaane Tu... Ya Jaane Na. He first appeared as a child actor in popular films such as Qayamat Se Qayamat Tak in 1988 and Jo Jeeta Wohi Sikandar in 1992. Since his debut as a lead actor in 2008, he has starred in a number of films like I Hate Luv Storys, Mere Brother Ki Dulhan and Delhi Belly. The notice to leave the country comes as Khan returns to acting this year with the Netflix film Adhure Hum Adhure Tum after a hiatus of over a decade. Image source, Imran Khan/Instagram Image caption, Khan also shared a photo from inside the detention van on his Instagram page On 10 October, the actor participated in the protest called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) - a wider GenZ-led movement that has been holding demonstrations for days seeking electoral reforms and the resignation of India's top election official over allegations of vote fraud. India's poll panel denies these charges. "Imran Khan had participated in the agitation despite not being an Indian citizen," police said in their statement. The complaint against Khan was lodged by Kirit Somaiya, a leader of India's and the state's governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), who accused the actor of being "involved in a conspiracy to spread anarchy in India". Khan did not address Somaiya's allegation directly, but had spoken to reporters about his participation in the protest. "I don't have demands. I'm here as a citizen, as a person who lives in this city. I'm here to see why freedom of movement is being restricted, why people's voices are being suppressed," he'd said. He added that he was not at the protest as the representative of any organisation. Following the protest, Khan was briefly detained by the police along with other protesters. He posted a photo of himself inside the police detention van on Instagram with the caption, "Apparently I'm going for a drive." The post received more than two million likes on the social media platform. Over the weekend, thousands of protesters had marched in Delhi, Mumbai and other parts of India, demanding the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar ahead of crucial state elections in response to the CJP's call. On Monday, leaders of many of India's main opposition parties, including Congress MP Rahul Gandhi, led thousands of protesters in a march from Connaught Place to the Supreme Court in Delhi. On Wednesday, two top CJP leaders were sent to jail for five days after being arrested for allegedly trespassing at a protest site in Delhi. The CJP has called for another protest on Friday evening in the capital. Related topics Bollywood Mumbai India Youth politics Asia

title: Albanian protests turn violent: What we know
page_title: Albanian protests turn violent: What we know  - BBC News
summary: Albania's capital Tirana has seen months of protests from an anti-government "Flamingo" movement, but what started on Tuesday this week was on a different scale.
text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Tirana has seen four days of clashes and the protests are spreading By Paul Kirby ,Â Europe Digital Editor Â and Â Paulin Kola Published 16 October 2026, 13:26 BST Updated 6 hours ago Protesters and anti-riot police have clashed in Albania's main cities in scenes not witnessed for decades. Government buildings have been attacked and some private businesses, too. So what is happening? How big and unusual are these protests? Albania's capital Tirana has seen months of protests from an anti-government "Flamingo" movement, but what started on Tuesday this week was on a different scale. And the clashes have spread beyond Tirana - to include the main cities of DurrÃ«s, ShkodÃ«r, LezhÃ« and Vlora in the west, GjirokastÃ«r in the south and KorÃ§Ã« in the east. The new demonstrations were announced as a student movement, ostensibly demanding action by the government to help with the high cost of education fees and books - and the higher cost of living. Secondary schools joined in, swelling the numbers. Before too long, masked protesters threw stones at police, and they responded with water cannon, tear gas and batons. Many were incensed by scenes of a young man being carried away, his broken leg dangling with him in agony. Apologies were expressed but failed to calm the situation. A floor of the education ministry was set on fire, with other government institutions ablaze, too. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, There have been violent scenes involving protesters and police in central Tirana Every evening, throughout the summer for some 135 days in a row, Albanians in central Tirana would hold pictures of a pink flamingo, calling on Prime Minister Edi Rama - now in his fourth term - to resign. The protests began over a mega-tourism project on the Adriatic coast linked to US President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner. Demonstrators said the bird would become extinct on an island near the coastal city of Vlora, if the plans for a luxury development went ahead. The public anger comes as allegations of corruption among ministers and other senior officials grow louder. One deputy prime minister has fled the country, another has been ordered to step down as investigations continue. Image source, Bloomberg via Getty Images Image caption, For almost five months over the summer, Albanians carrying images of flamingoes called on the prime minister to resign Student protesters attack government buildings in Albania Published 2 days ago 'Flamingo Revolution' takes off as thousands demand Albanian PM's resignation Published 4 July Kushner-backed luxury resort plan sparks protests in Albania Published 4 June So has the Flamingo movement radicalised? The flamingo protesters say they have no links to any political party - one of their slogans being "Rama in jail, Berisha in jail". While Rama is prime minister, Sali Berisha is Albania's main opposition leader - as well as a former prime minister and president. They were attended by young and old, parents with children and sometimes their grandparents. Some of the participants took pride in cleaning up after every night. But after months and an unusually hot summer, their numbers dwindled - with no sign that the government was meeting their demands. The current movement appears far more violent. Dozens of police have been hurt, and the eyes of Europe are now watching what happens next in a country viewed as one of the top candidates for EU membership. Several young protesters told the BBC that what was going on now was a new phase born of the previous movement. Five months of peaceful protest had been "met with humiliation, ridicule, mockery," complained one young woman called Livia. "That was a clear message from the government that our voice will not be allowed to be heard." Another called Brunela told the BBC's What in the World programme she was worried about what might happen next: "I am very terrified because the media and the government is reacting, especially now. It was not just my voice, it is the voice of Albanian youth." An overlap between the two sets of protests may well have occurred, even though flamingo leaders have not publicly stated so and no representative of the student movement has come forward. After all, their main concerns relate to corruption, which the prime minister says must be investigated by the justice system. How is the government handling the unrest? Rama has been touring some of the damaged buildings and blaming Sali Berisha for instigating chaos. "All of this is the work of the very same hand - the hand that has gripped the Albanian opposition by the throat, the hand that has burned and destroyed Albania more than once, and is now prepared to burn and destroy it again to prevent any progress. It is a blind struggle, fuelled by the most irrational hatred," he said on Friday. The prime minister has ruled out resigning, promising to "listen, address legitimate concerns and keep Albania moving forward". Berisha's Democratic Party has often tried to get people out to oust Rama. But the number of his loyal supporters, who have also protested for months and at times clashed with police, has been low in comparison to the current attendance. So there is some scepticism about Berisha's ability to mastermind the trouble, though he may well seek to capitalise on it. On the other hand, the Albanian media have suggested that secret services of foreign countries may be involved. Unfounded allegations have been made against Serbia, with commentators suggesting Belgrade is envious of Albania being often cited as potentially next in line to join the EU. Indeed, without mentioning names, Prime Minister Rama echoed the allegation on Friday. "These are foreign hands that do not wish for Albania to be at peace... they do not want Albania to be part of the united European family," he said, adding: "Do you think it is a coincidence that every time Albania receives another green light... or draws closer to that great ambition - that historic objective - flames suddenly erupt? It is no coincidence at all! None of what is happening now is a coincidence." Is Albania safe to visit? Although the street violence has taken place in many cities, it remains contained for the time being. The UK government has urged visitors to check media , external for latest information, stay away from "demonstrations, large-scale gatherings or political rallies" and follow advice of local authorities. Albania is a popular tourist destination, and the government in Tirana has warned that violence tarnishes the country's image, affecting both tourism and its European path. title: Are student protests being manipulated ahead of France's presidential election?
page_title: Are student protests being manipulated ahead Franceâs presidential election? - BBC News
summary: France's prime minister has suggested that student anger is being weaponised, as the unions and other protesters prepare to take to the streets too.
text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, The French prime minister has accused the radical left of weaponising the high school movement for electoral advantage By Katya Adler Europe Editor Published 16 October 2026, 00:25 BST The French passion for protest is legendary in Europe. Over the last few years, we have regularly witnessed farmers angry about costly regulations lobbing manure at local mayoral offices, while masked youths periodically hurl homemade grenades at riot police in disadvantaged city suburbs. For over three weeks now, thousands of students have barricaded entry to high schools and taken their grievances to the streets. This Saturday, hundreds of new demonstrations have been announced across France. Students are expected to be joined by workers' unions and key figures from the so-called "yellow vest" movement. France's Prime Minister, SÃ©bastien Lecornu, suggested this week that student anger was being manipulated as politics heats up ahead of next year's presidential election. The gilets jaunes (yellow vests) demonstrated against cost-of-living hikes for over a year from 2018 - becoming one of the longest-lived protest movements in French history. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, JÃ©rÃ´me Rodrigues (R) played a leading role in the gilets jaunes movement several years ago JÃ©rÃ´me Rodrigues, a prominent gilets jaunes activist, has used Instagram to encourage people to join Saturday's demonstrations. The protests should give a voice to those who "want to be able to live decently, no longer have to count every cent, and no longer have to choose between eating and driving", he said in a video. "Anger has no political party. An empty fridge has no political party," he added. So what is going on in the EU's second largest economy? Social unrest, government borrowing costs at eye-watering highs, a deeply divided French parliament and an apparent revolving door of exasperated French prime ministers - six prime ministers over the last five years - all claiming to want to reduce their country's public debt. Is France at breaking-point - and what does this all mean for the eurozone currency the French are such a huge part of? Figure caption, Watch: 'If we don't scream, they won't listen to us', student protester tells BBC in Paris "You can't compare France to the Greece debt crisis of 2012 or Argentina in 2001. And the financial markets know it," economist Anne-Laure Delatte told me. She is a CNRS Tenured Researcher at the Economics Department of Paris Dauphine University; a well-known face in debates on French media on the parlous state of the country's public debt. "The markets recognised already in 2024 that we would have a budgetary problem after [snap] elections left parliament deeply divided between three [opposing political] blocs but they also realise France is a big country with the ability to raise taxes if necessary." "Our situation is more like the UK in 2023 with Liz Truss," suggests Delatte, referring to the then UK prime minister's so-called mini budget, which triggered a sharp drop in the pound, a spike in government bond yields and soaring mortgage rates. "The crisis was relatively short-lived because the markets recognised the UK had the financial tools to right itself." "Here in France it would be painful, but a 4% increase in VAT would raise the 120bn euros needed to plug government debt. Investors know that," she concludes. Maybe, in theory. And, as Delatte also points out, the European Central Bank would likely intervene if France's finances nosedived to the point where other European economies would be affected. But with so many French citizens already visibly unhappy with the status quo, imagine the reaction if taxes were to increase, or welfare and education budgets decrease, further. France's national motto is libertÃ©, Ã©galitÃ©, fraternitÃ© (freedom, equality and fraternity), but that is certainly not the sense you get on seething streets and in viral social media posts. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Radical-left LFI leader Jean-Luc MÃ©lenchon (C) has been accused of exploiting the student protests ahead of next year's elections I met 17-year-olds Maxime, Madeleine and Elodie this week, perched on big green dustbins that have been used to block the entrance to their high school as part of the weeks' long protest. They told me things were bad enough here, in the 3rd district of Paris, with holes in classroom walls, swelling class sizes and a dearth of teaching staff, but the teenagers were more than aware, they said, that the situation was far worse in their capital city's disadvantaged suburbs. "France likes to speak of Ã©galitÃ© ," they told me "but the reality is the poor here are prejudiced against, while the rich benefit." None of them will be old enough to vote in the presidential election in France next spring but they questioned whether the changing face of politicians in power made all that much difference anyway. The three young women told me large-scale protests seemed the only way to get heard by French authorities. More on this story 'Everyone hates the police' â what France's school protests reveal about a divided nation Published 6 days ago France's school protests: What lies behind the anger Published 8 October France halts use of stun grenades after boy's hand blown off in student protests Published 7 October They are part of a defiant French tradition. Cultural icon Victor Hugo, the 19th-Century author of French Revolution classic Les MisÃ©rables , also an activist for the French Republic, proclaimed: " Si vous n'Ãªtes pas contents, manifestez, criez, hurlez, mais ne subissez pas ." ("If you are not happy, protest, shout, scream but do not give up and give in.") Amongst crowds of protesting students walking through Paris on Thursday, I came across a number of mums, with placards around their necks, reading: "Mums in solidarity." Were they there to protest or to protect their kids, I asked? "Both!" was the emphatic response. Gwen, 37, said she and other mothers were taking it in turns every morning to co-ordinate between students and police at their local school lock-in. This came after mounting accusations of police brutality, denied by France's interior ministry, during protests earlier this month in which hundreds were injured and a 15-year-old boy in the town of Lens lost a hand. France's interior minister has since suspended the use of stun grenades by police at high school demonstrations. Gwen told me she did not mind that her son was missing weeks of school as a result of the lock-ins. "It's a far better education for him to wake up to his civic duty and to fight for what is just in society," she said. At Thursday's demo I also came across 17-year-old Lola and her mother, Sandrine, sharing a placard that said revolution was the most beautiful expression of humanity. Image caption, Lola (R) was joined in the protest by her mother Sandrine, who had been part of the 1968 student movement "My mum took to the streets in '68," Lola said proudly. "Now it's my turn. No point in waiting for the presidential election in France. We want change now." Student protests in Paris in May 1968 are the stuff of legend in France. Demands for better education inspired workers to join the marches which turned into the Â­biggest general strike in French Â­history. It set the standard for revolutionary upheaval for a generation and is credited with creating new opportunities for the French left. Now, though, with six months to go before an already fraught presidential election in France, there are accusations that the hard left, under presidential hopeful Jean-Luc MÃ©lenchon, is weaponising student frustration. "Members of [MÃ©lenchon's] France Insoumise (LFI) are instrumentalising the high school movement for their electoral advantage," said SÃ©bastien Lecornu on Wednesday. He accused them of encouraging protests, then going through the motions of condemning any violence. "This hypocrisy damages France," said Lecornu. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, French Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu has complained that the high school protests are turning into a "movement of urban violence" But "MÃ©lenchon for President!" is a chant you often hear amongst the students in the streets. Supporters applaud his desire for a wealth tax in France, for lowering the voting age to 16 and for being the only presidential candidate to turn up to French schools to examine the state of them, several demonstrators told me. For Marine Le Pen, the nationalist anti-immigration favourite in France's presidential race, the solution is cutting the country's â¬11bn contribution to the EU's budget. There is, though, reason to doubt that any new French president, from the left or the right, will be able to break the impasse over France's finances. France is far from alone in Europe right now faced with an ageing population, a generous welfare state to run and a national economy squeezed by outside pressures such as US President Donald Trump's trade tariffs and the war in the Gulf. Whether in France, Germany, Sweden or Italy, there is an inherent tension between politicians who hesitate to tell voters the truth about shrinking public finances, the defence establishment's demand for higher defence spending and citizens' insistence on improved public services. In France, that pressure is particularly acute. French public expenditure, at about 57% GDP, is one of the steepest amongst wealthy nations worldwide. Social spending, particularly on pensions, is exceptionally large, while French citizens pay one of the highest overall tax and social contribution burdens in Europe. Simply put, they expect a welfare and public service bang for their buck. But economist Anne-Laure Delatte does not believe having a new president will ease her country's financial migraine. "We need constitutional change. A new system. A new Republic," she told me. "Our Fifth Republic is centred around a powerful president. Parliament is there to block him or her rather than to find consensus or to make new laws." For France to progress, she says, that has to change. The French parliamentary election that follows the 2027 presidential vote is likely to be as divided as ever, she believes: "We need a system where MPs have more power and should learn consensus and coalition-building from our European neighbours." In her opinion, education had to be protected and funds better distributed. It was an investment in France's financial future, she told me. "Our current system of inequality in schooling and low wages for teachers means we lose out from benefiting from the best and brightest across French society. That is not only unfair on individuals but our economy ultimately loses out on innovation and productivity." Re-writing France's constitution is not on the cards, at the moment. So, what about the here and now, I asked centrist politician Anne-Catherine Loisier. She's a senator for the Centrist Union in France's upper house of parliament and vice president of the parliamentary group for sciences and technology. Image caption, Senator Anne-Catherine Loisier believes the solution lies in decentralising power away from Paris Loisier, along with pretty much every leading French politician across the political spectrum, says the protesting students "must feel heard". "Our budgets are limited," she admitted, "but you don't necessarily need more money. You can make improvements by redistributing funding better. Education is a regional competence in France. Every region should take a look at local needs and address priorities accordingly. That action can be taken immediately." I asked Loisier if she agreed with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, the former mayor of Greater Manchester, that regions should be given greater powers. "Absolutely," she replied. "France has traditionally been very Paris-centric but so much could be improved by decentralising the country." "My France isn't broken. I don't recognise that image you see portrayed in the media. My country is made up of lots of Frances. Paris, the regions; northern and southern France. We need to give power back to the people. Local governments can look people in the eye directly, so voters feel they have power over their own future, rather than politicians handing them their fate from up high in Paris." "That way I hope we can restore voters' - and students' - faith in politics." It's a promise you hear from politicians - right and left - ahead of France's huge elections next year. But opinion polls here, as across most of Europe, indicate public faith in the political class is in dwindling supply. Related topics France Europe Paris Students

title: At least 33 pupils and teacher killed after school roof collapses in Pakistan
page_title: Peshawar: At least 33 pupils and teacher killed after Pakistan school roof collapses  - BBC News
summary: Children were buried under the debris after the roof crashed through three classrooms, police say.
text: Figure caption, On the ground in Pakistan as school roof collapse kills more than 30 children By Bilal Ahmed and Azizullah Khan ,Â BBC Urdu ,Â Reporting from Peshawar Â and Â Phelan Chatterjee Published 15 October 2026 At least 33 pupils and a teacher have been killed after a school roof collapsed in the north-western Pakistani city of Peshawar, according to hospital officials. More than a dozen others are injured, with some in a critical condition. Emergency services were called to the private Al-Khair school in Dir Colony at 08:48 (03:48 GMT) on Thursday after lessons had begun, rescue official Bilal Faizi told the BBC. The roof of an upper-floor classroom had collapsed, he said, causing ceilings below to cave in and trap children beneath the debris. Announcing the arrest of the school's owner, police chief Mian Saeed promised a thorough inquiry into "whether there were any violations of building codes". Warning: This article contains distressing details An English teacher from a nearby school said he immediately rushed to the site with other local residents when they heard sirens and the sound of ambulances. Together, they pulled more than 20 children from the rubble, he said. "I personally pulled out six children with my own hands. Most of them were alive and talking. But later it was found that they had passed away." "There was a lot of blood," he said. "One child said he was in a lot of pain. His tongue had dried up in his mouth, [and he was] asking for water." Sohail, another local resident, said he and others tried to remove children from under the rubble "using shovels". Image source, Reuters Image caption, A rescue worker said an upper-floor roof collapsed, crashing through three classrooms The school building had been constructed on a temporary basis, according to emergency official Arif Khattak. Earlier reports suggested the destroyed classrooms were in a two-storey part of the building, but Peshawar police chief Mian Saeed later confirmed that classrooms on three floors had been brought down. There were about 30 pupils in the top class, 40 in the middle and 45 on the ground floor, he said. It appears that when the roof of the top-floor classroom collapsed, the falling rubble crashed through classrooms below, bringing their ceilings down too. Saeed said the entire structure, which had "substandard" roof slabs, was "overloaded" and beyond the limit of how much weight it could bear. The school is on a very narrow street, meaning it was difficult for rescue workers to reach the site and transport the injured to hospitals. Peshawar's Lady Reading Hospital reported the deaths of 32 children and a teacher while Naseerullah Khan Babar Memorial Hospital reported one child dead. The police chief said the building was still "extremely dangerous" and urged people to move away. The Governor of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Faisal Karim Kundi, has ordered a safety audit of all schools in the province to "identify potential risks and ensure that immediate corrective measures are taken wherever necessary". "We cannot allow the safety of our children to be compromised," he said. Furious family members of deceased pupils accused the school of ignoring safety concerns. "Make an example of them, a lesson for all," Mohammad Zaman, a man who lost two nephews in the disaster, told Reuters news agency. Image source, Reuters Image caption, The roof crashed through three classrooms and buried schoolchildren in debris, police say Image source, Reuters In June, fourteen children died after the roof of a private tuition centre near Lahore collapsed. And in August, 14 newborn babies were killed by a fire that ripped through a neonatal unit at a hospital in the capital, Islamabad, which an inquiry found lacked fire alarms and sprinklers . title: At the Brooklyn shop in 'surreal' row with Kelly Clarkson over mechanical bird
page_title: Inside Brooklyn novelty shop at centre of 'surreal' row with Kelly Clarkson over mechanical bird - BBC News
summary: Art of Play says its staff have been threatened after the singer complained online about how she was treated.
text: Figure caption, Watch: What's going on between Kelly Clarkson and a Brooklyn store bird? By Madeline Halpert New York Published 14 October 2026 On a rainy Wednesday afternoon, a novelty toy and games store in a quiet part of New York City was seeing much busier foot traffic than usual. Inside, the shop was packed with cameramen and customers, while passersby in this Brooklyn neighbourhood of Cobble Hill looked inside, asking: "Where's the bird?" Art of Play has found itself at the centre of a social media storm since the weekend when Grammy-winning musician Kelly Clarkson complained online that the boutique store would not let her buy a singing and dancing mechanical bird that was perched on the wall. The Since U Been Gone singer claimed she was "looked at as if I couldn't afford" the bird - which she said had a price tag of $15,000 (Â£11,000). "Y'all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts' character in Pretty Woman," she said, referring to a scene from the 1990 romantic comedy film where Roberts' character is treated poorly by staff at a shop, who imply she cannot afford various items. In a follow-up post on social media, Clarkson said the store had told her the bird cost $15,000 and that they could find her something else "comparable". Art of Play has defended how it treated the star on social media, saying the wooden bird - which is called Molly - is permanently attached to the wall and is not for sale. It said that during Clarkson's five-minute visit on Saturday, an employee suggested to her that she could buy an identical bird for $15,000. They also said they had offered her a different singing bird for $2,000 from a clock-making shop in Germany, which she could have purchased that day. "Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by eight million people who have never visited our store," Art of Play said. "It's been a surreal experience to be the focus of such widespread outrage after just one mention by a celebrity." Image caption, Molly the mechanical bird now has a price tag of $15m Clarkson defended her decision to criticise the store on social media, saying: "I never blast people but you my friend were an exception." When the BBC visited the store on Wednesday, there were more reporters than customers. A shopkeeper said they would not comment on the story anymore and just wanted to get back to business as usual. Molly still hung on the wall at the shop, this time next to a price tag of $15m. The sign jokes that the sculpture is the "world's most famous singing bird automata!" The store's owner has said he and his staff have faced threats and harassment after Clarkson's complaint, telling the BBC's US partner CBS News that the singer had endangered them. This week, a man filmed himself yelling expletives outside the store, before accusing its employees of "racially profiling" Clarkson. Image caption, Customer Emily Trantanella likes Art of Play The kerfuffle lingered in headlines on Wednesday as a news outlet released surveillance video from Art of Play purporting to show Clarkson's visit. The grainy footage, which has no audio, is said to show her wearing a yellow shirt, a baseball cap and a backpack while browsing items, including Molly the bird. She can be seen talking with an employee - apparently about the bird as she points at it - and later moving to leave the store. She comes back in to say something animatedly to the cashier. But while the argument over the bird has gone viral online, some of Art of Play's customers had not heard about it before being greeted by news cameras on the premises. One customer who was in town visiting his daughter said he was not familiar with the controversy. For others, Clarkson's claims that those at the store had treated her rudely came as a surprise. Kiran Ramineni, who lives next door, described Art of Play as a "very nice small mom and pop store" and said he had seen flocks of journalists there in recent days. Shopgoer Emily Trantanella, 27, said: "I feel like a pretty woman and I've always been treated very well here. "I really like it here." Related topics United States Birds

title: Brazil's Congress approves shorter working week in win for Lula
page_title: Brazil's Congress approves shorter working week in win for Lula - BBC News
summary: Lula's supporters hope the measure will boost his popularity ahead of a presidential run-off in 10 days.
text: Image source, Cris Faga/NurPhoto via Getty Images Image caption, The measure had broad support and trade unions held rallies in its favour in recent weeks By Vanessa BuschschlÃ¼ter ,Â Latin America online editor ,Â Mariana Schreiber ,Â BBC News Brasil in Brasilia Â and Â Vitor Tavares ,Â BBC News Brasil in SÃ£o Paulo Published 15 October 2026 Brazil's Congress has approved a constitutional amendment that will cut the working week from 44 hours to 40 and give employees two days off per week without cutting their salary. The change represents the biggest overhaul to workers' rights since Brazil's return to democracy in 1988. Senators passed the amendment, which left-wing President Luiz InÃ¡cio Lula da Silva had championed, less than two weeks before a second round in the Latin American nation's presidential election. Lula's supporters are hoping that its passage, which is estimated to benefit more than 30 million workers, will boost his chances of closing in on his right-wing rival, FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro, in the 25 October run-off. The son of former President Jair Bolsonaro won the first round of the presidential election with 47% of the vote, ahead of Lula on 45.2%. Both fell short of the 50% of valid votes needed to stave off a decisive second round. Opinion polls suggest that the move to cut the working week is very popular, with one nationwide survey finding that almost 70% of Brazilians backed it. The measure had already passed in the Chamber of Deputies, Brazil's lower house, in May, before senators overwhelmingly backed the measure on Wednesday by 75 votes to one. FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro, who is currently a senator, dropped his previous opposition to the measure and also cast a "yes" vote. Announcing his change of heart on Tuesday, he argued that he had been swayed by the measure's popularity, commenting: "Most Brazilian workers âwant to â see the end of the six-day workweek, so I'm going to vote in favour of ending it." The younger Bolsonaro had earlier denounced the proposal as an "opportunistic" attempt by his presidential rival to appeal to working-class voters. Before his about-turn, he had said that it should be down to employees and employers to agree on a work schedule, rather than restrictions being imposed by a constitutional amendment. Lula described Bolsonaro's policy reversal as "electoral opportunism" and celebrated the amendment's approval, saying it would make a real difference to workers. "It means more time to live, rest, be with family, watch your children grow up, look after yourself and enjoy life," he wrote on social media. Image source, MAURO PIMENTEL/AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Parent groups were among those to back the change Critics of the measure have warned that it will raise production costs, which will eventually be passed on to the consumer, resulting in higher prices. But its supporters argue that having two days off a week will allow workers to be better rested and therefore more productive in the hours that they do work. The change is due to be phased in, with the working week first being shortened to 42 hours after a two-month grace period and then again to 40 hours at a later stage. The changes will take more than a year to entirely take effect but many of its backers are already celebrating. Luciana de Almeida, 36, who works six days a week as a cashier in a supermarket, said it would "make a lot of difference" to her life. The single mother, who lives in Rio de Janeiro, said she has been missing out on time with her three children as the only day off she had was usually spent doing domestic chores. "My body, and my mind in particular, are very tired," she told BBC Brasil. "I need time with my daughters, have some leisure time, or even just some time resting at home." title: Bus hits train stopped on French side of Channel Tunnel, with 19 injured
page_title: Bus hits train stopped on French side of Channel Tunnel, with 19 injured - BBC News
summary: Two people were airlifted to hospital but no-one's life appeared to be in danger, officials said.
text: Figure caption, Watch: Emergency crews head towards Channel Tunnel crash By Patrick Jackson Â and Â Toby Mann Published 15 October 2026 A bus has hit a stationary freight train near the French entrance to the Channel Tunnel, injuring the driver and 18 passengers, French authorities say. The bus, which was carrying lorry drivers due to take a shuttle rail service, struck the train at the loading platform of the tunnel in Coquelles, near Calais, at 19:27 (18:27 BST) on Thursday. The bus driver and one passenger were severely injured and evacuated by helicopter. None of the injuries were life threatening, a local official said. Local sub-prefect Agathe Cury said freight and Eurostar passenger traffic through the tunnel had not been disrupted after a brief stoppage to evacuate injured people. An investigation has begun. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Trains near the French entrance to the Channel Tunnel (file image) "Two trains were on either side of the platform. One was being loaded by heavy goods vehicles ahead of a cross-Channel journey, and another train that had previously been loaded was departing," Cury said. "For a reason that currently remains unknown, the minibus collided with the departing train. "The bus did not overturn, it is still upright â but the shock and the collision caused injuries to the people involved." The incident involved a minibus transporting workers who were about to board Le Shuttle. All were men of different nationalities, she added. It is not clear whether any British nationals are among the injured. Cury said it was "the first time an incident of this type has occurred" on an Eurotunnel loading platform. The BBC's Evan Davis, who was travelling through the Eurotunnel to Calais at the time of the incident, witnessed blue light vehicles "concentrated on one of the platforms" as he entered France. "There were plenty of cars queueing up at check-in when I drove past just now, and I saw some cars going through check-in, so despite the collision they weren't being held," he said from the scene. Photos published by local French newspaper La Voix du Nord , external showed a small bus with damage to its front and side standing alongside a train, among a crowd of emergency workers. Eurostar has released an update saying: "An incident occurred several kilometers away from the Channel Tunnel. "This incident does not involved or impact Eurostar trains running from and to London. All of Eurostar trains will run as expected." The Eurotunnel runs under the sea between England and France, from Folkestone in Kent to Coquelles on the French side. Three different rail services operate through the tunnel - the Eurostar, a passenger train that begins in London and goes to several European destinations, freight trains which transport goods and Le Shuttle, which transports vehicles. title: China tells Israel to stop 'forced establishment' of West Bank settlements
page_title: China tells Israel to stop 'forced establishment' of West Bank settlements - BBC News
summary: Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi spoke to Israeli President Isaac Herzog on the sidelines of a conference.
text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, China has been positioning itself as a mediator for conflicts in the Middle East By Koh Ewe Published 16 October 2026, 09:45 BST Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi has told Israel to stop its "forced establishment" of settlements in the West Bank and reverse its actions, his office said. The "Palestinian question" is "the greatest historical injustice of this century", Wang told Israeli President Isaac Herzog in a face-to-face meeting on the sidelines of a conference in Azerbaijan on Thursday. Beijing has been a long-standing supporter of the Palestinian cause and has maintained that a "two-state solution" is the "correct direction". It has also been positioning itself as a mediator for conflicts in the Middle East. In 2023 Beijing brokered a deal to restore diplomatic ties between Iran and Saudi Arabia after years of hostility. Earlier this year, it was part of efforts, along with Pakistan, to propose a ceasefire in the US-Israel war against Iran . Beijing's efforts to tackle the war in Gaza have focused on Palestinian unity. In 2024 Beijing got rival Palestinian factions to agree to form an interim "national reconciliation government" for the occupied West Bank and Gaza after the war with Israel, although it was never implemented. Now, Wang says the "immediate priority" is to fully open access to Gaza and stop the continued spread of a "humanitarian catastrophe". China is willing to work with the international community to get the parties to return to dialogue and "seek a political solution to the conflict", he said. In a post on X, Herzog said he was "pleased" to meet Wang and their talk "focused on the relations between our countries and the situation in the Middle East". "I emphasised Israel's desire for peace in the region, alongside the strategic threats to our security, first and foremost from Iran and its terror proxies," he wrote. China maintains close ties with Iran and is the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, which had previously come under US sanctions because of Tehran's nuclear programme. China itself has been accused of trying to dilute its minority populations by encouraging Han Chinese migration to Tibet, which it annexed in the 1950s, and Xinjiang. Beijing rejects those claims, saying its policies promote economic development and social stability. One year into the ceasefire, people in Gaza continue to live under the regular threat of Israeli strikes, displacement and food security challenges. Although large-scale bombardment has stopped, Israel has continued strikes in Gaza almost every day . More than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli strikes there in the year since the ceasefire started in October 2025, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. The US-brokered ceasefire was the first phase of a deal to end the war in Gaza, which had been triggered by a deadly Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023. But progress into the deal's next phase has been stalled, with both Israel and Hamas accusing each other of violating the terms of their agreement. Related topics China Israel Asia

title: Dad fined after son, 2, died in Cyprus hotel fall
page_title: Essex dad sentenced after son died in Cyprus hotel fall - BBC News
summary: Joshua Foster "lost control" of his son while showing him the view of a water park from a window.
text: Image source, Press Association Image caption, Joshua Foster "lost control" of his son after placing him on a windowsill, a court in Cyprus heard By Lewis Adams Essex Published 16 October 2026, 10:31 BST Updated 6 hours ago A father whose two-year-old boy fell from a fourth floor window of a Cyprus hotel has been fined â¬3,000 (Â£2,500) for causing his death. Joshua Foster thought the window was closed when he placed his son on a sill to show him the view of a waterpark and "lost control" of him , Paphos District Court previously heard. The toddler fell nearly 40ft (12.1m) at the five-star King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort on 12 July, the first day of the family's holiday in Chlorakas. Foster, 37, from Essex, admitted causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act and was sentenced earlier. He told reporters afterwards: "Thank you for the support. I'm looking forward to going home and being with my wife and daughter." Later, the family said in a statement: "We are relieved that this process is now over, but for our family, the consequences of this tragedy will never end. "Our son was deeply loved and will be forever missed. His loss is something we carry with us every day." Foster, an auditor, arrived in Cyprus hours before the incident with his wife, two children and in-laws. They enjoyed various activities and swimming, before getting ready for dinner in the evening. Image source, Press Association Image caption, The incident happened on the first day of the family's holiday at the five-star King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort on the Mediterranean island's west coast At about 18:00, Foster, his father-in-law and son were walking towards a lift when the boy noticed a waterpark outside. Foster pushed the lift button, placed the child on the windowsill and the "inconceivable" unfolded before he could react, the court heard. The boy was taken to Paphos General Hospital and later pronounced dead. "The window did not appear to carry markings that would necessarily have alerted the defendant to the fact that one section was open," said District Judge Froso Christodoulidou. His failure to establish that the window was not closed led to the tragic result, the judge added. "It was a momentary error which created a dangerous situation with fatal consequences," he said. The judge added there was "no evidence that the defendant deliberately exposed the child to danger", according to a translation of proceedings. She added no sentence could outweigh the "personal consequences of the loss of his child". Image source, Press Association Image caption, Lawyer Alexandros Alexandrou said his client's remorse was "clear" In a voluntary statement to police, Foster said when he placed his son on the windowsill, the boy "fell before he had a chance to grab him". While Foster had alcohol in his system, it did not form a significant part of the case against him and his lawyer Alexandros Alexandrou said there was no testimony he was drunk. After the sentencing, Foster's lawyer, Alexandros Alexandrou, told reporters the case should have "never gone to court". He said Foster was held in custody for eight days immediately after the incident and he had to call his daughter from custody to explain what had happened. "Within this three months, there was a lost opportunity for this man to grieve as he wanted to, to be with his family," he said. He described his client as an "incredible father". "[He is] an exemplary family man with a beautiful family behind him, that support him, that embraces him, that has always been by his side." Do you have a story suggestion for Essex? title: Houthi missile attack on Yemeni presidential palace kills five, minister says
page_title: Houthi missile attack on Yemeni presidential palace kills five, minister says - BBC News
summary: Yemen's information minister says the prime minister and other ministers were unhurt when ballistic missiles hit al-Maashiq Palace.
text: Image source, UGC Image caption, Verified video footage showed smoke above the presidential palace in Aden By Orla Guerin ,Â Senior International Correspondent ,Â Reporting from Aden Â and Â David Gritten Published 15 October 2026 Updated 16 October 2026 00:38 BST Five people have been killed and 16 injured in a Houthi missile attack targeting the presidential palace in the port city of Aden in southern Yemen, which is the seat of the internationally-recognised government, officials say. Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani told the BBC that the prime minister and other ministers were unhurt when five ballistic missiles hit al-Maashiq Palace. The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said they struck "the Saudi enemy's military operations headquarters in Aden". A coalition led by Saudi Arabia backs the government and is providing air support for an offensive by pro-government forces against the Iran-backed Houthis. Yemeni health minister Qasim Buhaibeh said the casualties included "those working to guard the site and civilian employees". The country's Prime Minister Shaya Zindani condemned the Houthis' attack on Aden, calling it "cowardly" and a "continuation of their criminal behaviour". He said the government continued to carry out its duties and vowed that it would not weaken the resolve of its forces to continue operations against the Houthis on Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast and other front lines. Earlier, the Houthis denied that they had attacked Saudi Arabia on Thursday, after the coalition said its forces had intercepted a cruise missile in the Medina region, home to one of Islam's holiest shrines. The Houthis have been launching missiles and drones at airports, oil and gas facilities, and military bases in Saudi Arabia in retaliation for the strikes on the territory that they control in western Yemen, including the capital Sanaa. On Saturday, a Houthi missile strike killed 13 people at Riyadh's international airport, which was the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade. Saudi Arabia's deputy foreign minister accused Iran of encouraging the Houthis to escalate their conflict with the kingdom. "Iran continues to arm, train and support the Houthi militia in violation of UN Security Council resolutions," Rayed Krimly told reporters, according to AFP news agency. "We think that the escalation by the Houthis at this latest stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran," he added. There was no immediate response from Iran's government. However, it has previously denied supplying weapons to the Houthis and said it only supports them politically. Iran's foreign minister has also said it is ready to provide "any assistance necessary to facilitate the start of talks" between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis. Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the internationally-recognised government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule. A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. The conflict escalated in September after the Houthis seized part of Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for global shipping. Their advance contributed to a rise in oil prices following six months of war between the US, Israel and Iran. Last week, pro-government forces said they had regained control of territory overlooking Bab al-Mandab after launching a major counter-offensive with the support of Saudi air strikes. At least 1,282 people have been killed and 5,890 injured in the fighting in Yemen since 6 August, according to the government's health ministry. The UN says another 201,000 people have been displaced and that there has been an alarming surge in suspected cholera cases. title: India's 'cockroach' party founder detained ahead of protest
page_title: CJP, Abhijeet Dipke: 'Cockroach' party founder detained ahead of Central Park Delhi protest - BBC News
summary: The youth-led movement had called for a Delhi protest after mass detentions last week and the jailing of two leaders.
text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Abhijeet Dipke's youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has drawn thousands onto the streets in recent months By Zoya Mateen, Azadeh Moshiri & Vikas Pandey BBC News, Delhi Published 16 October 2026, 00:30 BST Updated 9 hours ago Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of India's "cockroach" movement, and a few others were detained in Delhi as police tried to stop a protest demanding the resignation of the country's election chief. Hundreds had gathered in Connaught Place, one of the capital's busiest commercial districts, waving Indian flags and shouting slogans despite a heavy security presence. Police sealed off Central Park, the planned site of the protest, and deployed thousands of police and paramilitary personnel to prevent the gathering. The Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) accuses India's Election Commission of manipulating voter lists to favour Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling BJP. Both deny the allegation. The group has held a series of protests in Delhi in recent weeks, with police repeatedly detaining its leaders and supporters. Friday's demonstration unfolded under similarly heavy security presence, though the police response was more restrained than during last weekend's sweeping crackdown. Hours before the protest, police went to the house where Dipke was staying. In an exchange broadcast live on Instagram, he challenged officers who had come to caution him against holding the march, asking whether waving the Indian flag was against the law. Hours later, the BBC saw officers surround Dipke as he approached his car and force him into a police vehicle. Some supporters tried to stop it from leaving. It was Dipke's second detention in less than a week. Last Saturday, police had boarded his plane shortly after it landed in Delhi to prevent him from reaching another demonstration. He was released the following day. The movement's two other main leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, were also detained last weekend and later released. But on Wednesday, they were sent to jail for five days after returning to Jantar Mantar, a protest site near parliament that police had recently declared off-limits. Friday's march was partly intended to demand the release of Das and Ranka. Dipke's detention means the movement's three main leaders are once again in custody. The CJP said it had lost contact with him and accused police of taking him to an undisclosed location and denying him access to lawyers. But they insist the arrests and detentions will not stop them. "They may detain three people, but how will they stop 30 tomorrow? How will they stop 300 leaders?" CJP spokesperson Mehr Pasricha told the BBC. Police have not publicly confirmed the grounds for Dipke's detention or responded to the CJP's latest allegations. Anish Gawande, the opposition politician who had been hosting Dipke, also questioned the police action. "Detaining a lone man walking with the national flag in his hand is a bit of a joke," he said. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Hundreds of people gathered in central Delhi to unfurl the national flag as part of the protest At Connaught Place, the police presence dwarfed the protest itself. Around 200-300 people initially gathered outside Central Park, which authorities had closed. Unable to enter, they walked around its perimeter, waving Indian flags and shouting slogans. More protesters arrived as the evening progressed. Officers kept emerging from buses parked around the district. Journalists crowded the streets too, and together with police, they far outnumbered the demonstrators. For much of the evening, police largely held back, with the BBC witnessing only a handful of detentions. But as darkness fell, officers began using force against some protesters. The BBC saw some young demonstrators being pushed into a bus where women were already being held. Inside were around 50 female officers, far more than the number of detainees. The BBC also saw two people being injured during the police action. One protester fell to the ground and appeared to have hurt their leg. Among those detained was Neha Bora , a prominent leader of the left-wing All India Students' Association (AISA) who has emerged as one of the faces of the recent protests. She had also been detained during last weekend's crackdown. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Student activist Neha Bora is among the people detained by the Delhi police on Friday evening Barely five months old, the CJP began as an online campaign in May after India's chief justice likened some unemployed young people to cockroaches. Dipke embraced the insult and turned it into a rallying cry. By July, the group had become a formidable force, drawing thousands of young people into protests over leaked exam papers. A march towards parliament in July descended into clashes with police, bringing the movement wider attention and intensifying pressure on the government. The unrest eventually forced the resignation of India's education minister. The CJP has since turned its attention to India's electoral system, demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a sweeping revision of voter lists known as the Special Intensive Revision (SIR). Critics say the exercise risks removing legitimate voters from the rolls, potentially depriving them of the right to vote. The Election Commission says it is targeting ineligible, dead and duplicate voters and denies allegations that it is favouring the ruling BJP. Last weekend, authorities imposed severe restrictions to stop CJP supporters from reaching a planned rally, sealing off roads, shutting metro stations and deploying thousands of security personnel across Delhi. The BBC witnessed , external dozens of protesters being detained across the capital, including students and journalists. The action drew criticism but police defended it as necessary to maintain public order and prevent unauthorised gatherings. Dipke, Das and Ranka were released the following day after agreeing to maintain peace and good behaviour. But the dispute over where they could protest was only beginning. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Delhi authorities have said Central Park is closed on Friday and Saturday for "administrative reasons" Police removed Jantar Mantar from Delhi's list of approved protest sites, naming three alternative venues. Built in the 18th Century to study the stars, the observatory stands close to Parliament and has long been one of India's most recognisable stages for public dissent. The CJP accused authorities of trying to push demonstrations away from the seat of power. On Tuesday, Das and Ranka returned to the restricted site with a handful of supporters, unfurling the Indian flag and shouting slogans against Kumar. Police said some protesters had climbed over a locked gate and that the organisers had breached the conditions of their release. The following day, the two men were sent to jail for five days. The arrests did little to deter the movement from announcing another demonstration. In a video message on Thursday, Dipke urged supporters unable to travel to Delhi to raise the Indian flag in their own towns and cities. He also acknowledged the possibility of being arrested again. "I also may be jailed after this, but I am not worried. Tricolour is my pride and I will raise it," he said. By Friday morning, police had served him with a notice warning against holding the march without permission. Authorities closed Central Park for two days, citing "administrative reasons", and offered to let a small group wave the national flag and sing the anthem at another location. The CJP came up with a different plan. Supporters were told to enter Connaught Place in groups of fewer than five, unfurl the flag, take a photograph and leave. "Waving the Tiranga is not a crime," the movement declared in a social media poster, using the Hindi name for India's tricolour. It urged supporters to share their photographs online. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Sporadic protests erupted around the Central Park on Friday evening despite the detentions Opposition parties have also been holding protests against Kumar and the Election Commission. Last week, Rahul Gandhi and other opposition lawmakers were detained while attempting to march to the commission's headquarters. They have also taken their concerns to President Droupadi Murmu and marched towards the Supreme Court. Gandhi has condemned the arrests of CJP leaders and called for Jantar Mantar to be reopened to protesters, although the opposition and the youth-led movement have largely demonstrated separately. Home Minister Amit Shah has accused the opposition of spreading falsehoods about the voter-list revision and defended the commission's independence. For the CJP, the immediate question is how long it can sustain its protests with its three main leaders in custody. Pasricha said the party had a team and a plan in place. "If the top three continue to stay behind bars, we will continue to protest peacefully," she said. Related topics India Delhi Youth unemployment Youth politics Asia

title: Inside Ukrainian offensive pushing Russia back - with Starlink playing a key role
page_title: Inside Ukrainian offensive pushing Russia back - with Starlink playing a key role - BBC News
summary: The BBC joins Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi as it regains crucial territory in the Donbas, but optimism has been dampened by souring relations with President Trump.
text: Figure caption, Watch: BBC follows Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi pushing Russia back on frontline By Dan Johnson Ukraine correspondent ,Â Reporting from near Lyman, eastern Ukraine Published 4 hours ago A Russian drone zips across the computer screen, startling the commanders keeping watch over the battlefield via a live stream in their bunker. Cigarette in one hand, radio in the other, one of them calls in their own drone to bring it down and warns the soldiers below of the threat. The men are dangerously exposed, on the long walk across open ground from their front line positions. They are being replaced after three months forcing the Russians back. This is part of Operation Vivaldi, a Ukrainian counter-offensive which they say has liberated 277 sq km (106 square miles) in the eastern Donbas region in recent months. The name reflects the offensive's four stages, or seasons - like the Italian composer's violin concerto. The successful assault blunted an attempted Russian pincer movement that threatened to encircle the key Fortress Belt cities still under Ukrainian control. While Russia this month pummels Ukraine from the air, crippling its energy infrastructure and killing scores of civilians across the country, at the front, it is Ukraine that has made recent gains. Kyiv says it has inflicted heavy losses - 8,000 Russian casualties in Vivaldi alone, and close to 50,000 along the front in the month of September â and suffered few casualties in return. Image source, Reuters Image caption, The Starlink system was integrated into Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi, but this week Kyiv said restrictions had been imposed on it without warning The Institute for the Study of War reported that pro-Russian military bloggers had acknowledged the Ukrainian advances, and expressed fears this could lead to more losses for Russia in the future. No Russian official has publicly acknowledged the Ukrainian gains. Russian ministry of defence briefings say only that they were "repelling attacks" in the Lyman region, or "improving the tactical position at the front". Despite Ukraine's forward moves, Russian drones are still ever-present. Phoenix, Commandant of the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unit, tells me his men face 10 on an average day. Image caption, Ukraine's military says it has liberated 277 sq km in the eastern Donbas region He is fixed on the live stream as a Ukrainian snare swoops in, hovers for a few seconds and drops a net on to the drone, dragging it from the sky. This Russian drone was for reconnaissance, but if it had locked on to the soldiers, another drone carrying explosives would have followed. This moment of peril illustrates the layers making up the modern battlefield. The command bunker receives live pictures from a hovering camera, while below a Ukrainian attack drone attacks another enemy spotter which would have called in more flying firepower. Integrated in all of this is Starshield, the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink satellite communications network, providing broadband connectivity across the battlefield. Ukraine said this week, as Operation Vivaldi concluded, that the system had restrictions imposed without warning, limiting their capability. Musk and media reports suggest the order may have come from the White House. While Ukraine is not wholly reliant on Starshield, it is a key tool in their arsenal, vital for interceptor and mid-range strike drones. And knowing this tool can be restricted without any warning or consultation has sparked major concern in Ukraine. Beneath the battle for aerial superiority, unmanned ground vehicles scurry back and forth delivering supplies, evacuating the wounded or, increasingly, leading the charge against the enemy. Everything here relies on digital connectivity - to see, to move, to fly, to communicate, to fire. But at the bottom of this stack, it is still human beings in trenches who are holding the ground. The weary soldiers have made it safely to the command post. After 95 days pushing forward on the front line there is an emotional reunion. Image source, Matthew Goddard/BBC Image caption, Dealer, a soldier in the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unit, just came off the front line An infantryman with the call-sign Dealer tells me he feels strong, but it is good to be finally heading home: "It's an impressive operation. Over three months, we moved positions four times." He tells me the most frightening threat was Russian drones, piloted remotely and determined to hunt down their target. Commandant Phoenix said the preparation for the offensive was "enormous". "The men trained for months. We had to completely restructure our approach because previously we had been defending, and now we had to go on the offensive." Robots and drones led the assault on Russian positions and, for the first time, remote-controlled explosive vehicles were dropped behind Russian lines - 250 Russians surrendered. According to Ukrainian commanders, their year-long campaign has freed 16 settlements from Russian occupation. Image source, Matthew Goddard/BBC Image caption, Phoenix, Commandant of the Revenge Brigade's Silver Trinity unit In Karpivka, a village occupied since April, the Ukrainians found one local resident remaining - 61 year old Volodymyr Zamota, the last man standing when his neighbours fled the Russian advance in 2025. He says he survived for eight months in total isolation. "As they say, hope dies last," he told me. "I'm the only person left in the whole village, and the village has been almost completely destroyed." "I thought I would live to old age without experiencing anything like this, but then it happened. It's a terrible tragedy". That devastation defines the region Ukraine has just recaptured. It's still too risky for residents to return, if they even have a home intact. But Ukraine's soldiers are celebrating this regained ground, the halted Russian advance and the future potential this operation may present. "The real value of this is securing advantageous positions, favourable lines, and a bridgehead that grants us a superior position," Andriy Hitt, Revenge Bridge chief of staff, explained. "This allows us to create the necessary conditions for subsequent successful operations, seize the initiative in battle, and plan future successful manoeuvresâ¦ each of these actions is a building block towards victory." Image source, Matthew Goddard/BBC Image caption, Nets now span roads in eastern Ukraine to protect from drones All this could be threatened by the limitations on US technology, and American intelligence. Relations between Kyiv and Washington are at an all-time low. This week President Zelensky said he felt "betrayed" by Donald Trump, while the US leader declared he was "not a fan" of his Ukrainian counterpart, saying he was harder to deal with than Vladimir Putin. Trump says Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries have hiked oil prices. Ukraine says the US and Israeli war against Iran is the cause. But despite the diplomatic divisions, among the soldiers we met, morale is high. Dealer says Operation Vivaldi has renewed his belief Ukraine can win the war. The unit is ensuring Volodymyr, Grandpa as they call him, has enough to eat - drones drop off food parcels on their way to feed soldiers at the front. I asked Volodymyr if he believed Ukraine could win. "Yes, of course I do. I would just like to know when it will happen, when all of this will finally end." Additional reporting by Kostas Kallergis and Anastasiia Levchenko Related topics War in Ukraine Ukraine Russia More on this story Zelensky says Ukraine has right to defend itself after Trump criticism Published 4 hours ago US senators call for investigation into Ukraine's Starlink restrictions Published 6 hours ago

title: Israeli settlers attack Palestinians in West Bank during olive harvest
page_title: Israeli settlers attack Palestinians in West Bank during olive harvest - BBC News
summary: Israeli settlers were seen attacking Palestinian farmers and setting fire to olive trees in the West Bank.
text: Israeli settlers attack Palestinians in West Bank during olive harvest Israeli settlers attack Palestinians in West Bank during olive harvest Close The BBC has witnessed Israeli settlers attack Palestinians and set fire to olive trees in the occupied West Bank. title: Letters with 'suspicious substances' sent to US senators and election offices
page_title: Letters with 'suspicious substances' sent to US senators and election offices - BBC News
summary: A number of states have confirmed they were targeted by the mailings, including Oklahoma, Ohio and Louisiana.
text: Image source, Los Angeles Times via Getty Images By Grace Eliza Goodwin Published 15 October 2026 Federal authorities say they are investigating "potentially hazardous" letters containing "suspicious substances" that have been sent to congressional and state election offices around the US. The FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service (USPIS) said they were trying to trace the "suspicious mailings", some of which were intercepted before they were received. Authorities declined to say how many offices had been targeted, but several secretaries of state and congressional offices reported receiving the letters. Coming just weeks before the US midterm elections, it echoes previous security scares involving suspicious mail. The suspicious letters were sent to at least five Democratic senators' offices, most of which were intercepted before delivery. They include California's Alex Padilla, Connecticut's Chris Murphy and New York's Kirsten Gillibrand, the senators' offices confirmed to the BBC. New York Senator Chuck Schumer and Delaware Senator Lisa Blunt Rochester were also sent the suspicious pieces of mail, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News. "This incident is a stark reminder of the very real danger facing those who serve the public and who help administer our elections in the face of increasingly hostile political rhetoric," Padilla said in a statement to the BBC. Several state offices have also received the suspicious mailings. Delaware's Department of Elections said its office received and opened a letter containing a white powdery substance on Thursday, adding that staff followed security protocols on handling suspicious mail. The Oklahoma State Election Board and the Louisiana secretary of state both said this week that their offices had received letters containing a white powder. The Louisiana office was evacuated after a staff member opened the package on Tuesday, but it has since reopened after law enforcement found no evidence of harmful substances. Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose said his office was the intended recipient of a letter containing white powder, but the USPIS had intercepted it. The New York State Capitol in Albany and the Wyoming State Capitol in Cheyenne also received suspicious packages, according to emergency responder scanner feed reviewed by the BBC. "This FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service will continue to safeguard the public and secure elections for American citizens," the agencies said in a statement on Thursday. The suspicious mailings come just weeks before election day, which will determine the balance of power in Congress. Ahead of the 2024 election, vote officials in 17 states received suspicious packages . A year earlier, suspicious envelopes, some laced with fentanyl, were sent to election offices in at least five states. title: Maduro pleads not guilty to new torture-related charges in New York
page_title: Maduro pleads not guilty to additional charges in New York - BBC News
summary: "I reject this document entirely," Maduro said in court, responding to newly added torture-related charges.
text: Image source, REUTERS/Jane Rosenberg Image caption, Ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, are seen in a federal court in New York in July. By Kayla Epstein Reporting from in court in New York Published 15 October 2026 Venezuela's former leader NicolÃ¡s Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, appeared in court on Thursday to plead not guilty to new charges of conspiracy to commit torture. The US government initially accused Maduro of narco-terrorism, drug trafficking and weapons-related offenses, before adding new charges against him and Flores last week. Maduro and Flores were captured in January during a US military raid, after which they were taken to New York, where they remain in jail. The couple has pleaded not guilty to the allegations and both have argued to have the case thrown out on the grounds that they qualify for sovereign immunity. Their trial is scheduled for June 2027. In a new indictment last week, government prosecutors alleged Maduro and Flores "created and maintained a violent system of repression" that saw "thousands of Venezuelans" killed, harassed, and tortured. Nicolas Maduro denied the new charges brought against him by the US government, telling a court on Thursday he denied the "false accusations and false testimony against me." "I reject this document entirely," Maduro said in Spanish through a translator. Judge Alvin Hellerstein interrupted Maduro, and declared the court would enter a plea of not guilty for Maduro. "I am completely innocent. I am not guilty," Flores said through a translator. Maduro and Flores wore beige jail uniforms and both appear to have lost weight during their detention in Brooklyn. The alleged torture methods included "electric shock, asphyxiation, rape, forced nudity, prolonged isolation, starvation, punishment cells, and psychological torture", the indictment states. The US also accused Maduro of authorising the use of torture "against specific individuals" and alleges US citizens were tortured under this system. Prosecutors already have accused Maduro, his wife and son, and their accomplices of engaging in a cocaine-trafficking conspiracy and partnering with cartels designated as terrorist groups. Maduro previously called such charges a tool to further "imperial" plans for getting access to Venezuela's rich oil reserves. He and his wife's lawyers have argued that Maduro is the leader of a sovereign country and therefore immune from prosecution. They contend the US taking him by force is illegal. Flores unsuccessfully petitioned a judge to allow her to be released on bond while she awaited trial, arguing she had heart problems and other health issues while detained at the notorious Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn.
