title: Obama says drift towards extremism 'not inevitable'
page_title: Barack Obama tells Glasgow audience drift towards extremism 'not inevitable' - BBC News
summary: More than 12,000 people filled a major venue in the city to hear the former US president's take on the challenges the world is facing. .
text: Image source, PA Media Image caption, Barack Obama warned that online platforms were stoking anger and fear in people By Jonathan Geddes Published 15 October 2026 Barack Obama has told an audience in Glasgow that hope is worth fighting for despite big challenges facing the modern world. The 44th president of the United States said online platforms had shifted in recent years to focus on content that stoked anger and fear, but he believes a drift to extremism is "not inevitable". The comments came as he addressed an OVO Hydro crowd of 12,150 people while in conversation with British journalist and author Sathnam Sanghera, part of three speaking dates in the UK. He reflected on his time in the White House and examined the political and social challenges facing the US and the wider world. More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland More stories from Scotland Obama said that during his presidential campaign in 2008, when social media and technology was gaining traction, he had seen them as a beacon for hope But he said the same positive forces and tools that could mobilise people around democracy or human rights could also be used by hate groups. He said they "connected people for good, but also for ill". "It turns out that the reptilian side of our brain really gets attracted to anger, fear, resentment and the sense that someone is out to get you," he said. "So a lot of social media and a lot of our information is informed around that." But the former president, who has already spoken in Belfast and will appear in Manchester on Thursday night, said that a drift towards extremism was "not inevitable". He added: "After World War Two, at least in the United States and certainly in Europe as well, the federal government said 'we're going to set up some rules because we've seen what propaganda can do in the hands of somebody like Hitler. "We can see how big lies and misinformation can distort and enrage and incite violence. So we're going to hold these folks responsible'." "We have not chosen to do that." Image source, PA Media Image caption, The former President was speaking at the OVO Hydro Obama, who was president until 2016, said there was a "critical balance" that must be struck between free speech and regulation. But the 65-year-old said that the world and its leaders are going to need to find mechanisms and new institutions to allow rigorous debate and disagreement while helping people sort out basic facts. He said: "If I had a blame pie for why politics is so polarised and why we're seeing a rise of populism in many places, it's because of that information that is going into our brains every day." Obama said this resulted in young people feeling discouraged, and that "it's not a healthy diet that our brains are on at the moment". He added that he feared this could become even worse with AI making it hard to distinguish between what is true and what is not, something he believes will make democracy hard to function. Obama says people forget lessons from the past Speaking about hope, Obama was asked if he still believed in a Martin Luther King Jr phrase he quoted years ago, about the arm of the moral universe being long, but ultimately bending towards justice. The former president said that he still stands by the quote and argued that hope is an active "almost theological" choice people must make. He said: "It is a decision about how do we face and embrace this finite amount of time we have on the planet." He told the audience he believes it is healthier for people to believe that change is possible. "I think when we act on that basis, it doesn't always work out, but over time things do get better," he said. Obama also said there seems to be a cycle in humanity where people forget lessons learned from the past and start to take things for granted. "We start thinking 'maybe using language in public from our politicians that fosters hatred and scapegoats certain people â immigrants, Jews, or blacks or gays â that's just talk, it's humour'." He said people forget where that can lead to, with them becoming less tolerant. Obama told the audience that the world is going to be dealing with "big challenges", but he said he thinks "we can be better" and that making the world better remains worth fighting for. title: Palestinians and US journalist injured by Israeli settlers in West Bank harvest attack
page_title: Palestinians and US journalist injured by Israeli settlers in West Bank harvest attack - BBC News
summary: The BBC sees masked settlers attack Palestinians trying to harvest olives, amid a surge in similar incidents.
text: Figure caption, Watch: Israeli settlers attack Palestinians in West Bank during olive harvest By Lucy Williamson Middle East correspondent ,Â Reporting from Abu Falah Published 6 hours ago Dozens of masked settlers have attacked Palestinians and set fire to cars and olive trees during the annual olive harvest in the occupied West Bank. A BBC team witnessed one of several attacks in farmland near the Palestinian village of Abu Falah. A local official said the attacks had injured 12 Palestinians, including four dual Palestinian American citizens. A foreign journalist was also among those hurt. Driving into the area early in the morning, we came across the first signs of the violence : a stream of cars carrying wounded Palestinian olive farmers racing out along the narrow stony track, piled high with olive picking equipment, as smoke rose from several fires nearby. The bloodied face of Majdi Fheed peered out from the backseat of one car. "We were getting our olive trees and almost 15 Jewish guys â¦ started attacking us with guns, with rocks, with special weapons. They hit me on my head [and] my neck â look, I am bleeding!" Yaser AlKam, a council member from the neighbouring village of Turmus Aya told me Majdi - an American citizen - was attacked by settlers with nail-studded sticks, and needed treatment for deep wounds on his head. His elderly mother was also injured. Another man ferrying the injured to hospital told us that settlers had attacked them with sticks while they harvested their olives, and had burned three cars â including one of his own. "As soon as we got to the land and put our things on the ground, they started to come, so we ran away" said a woman next to him. Image caption, Several Palestinian-American citizens and a foreign journalist were left injured following the attacks Asked about the violence, a US State Department spokesperson said they were aware of the reports. "Weâ¯condemn criminalâ¯violenceâ¯by any partyâ¯in the West Bank and call for investigations, arrests, and convictions,â¯of those responsible," the spokesperson said. Watching the vehicles stream past her, 73-year-old Imm Khaldoun told me emphatically that, no matter what happened, she would always return to her land. "This is my land. It's my right [to be here]" she told me. The UN says the past two weeks have already seen more attacks by violent Israeli settlers than during the entire harvest season last year. Olive picking in the West Bank is now a test of speed, with trees rapidly stripped of fruit as soon as the sun rises, before violent Israeli settlers attack. In another olive orchard nearby, we watched as dozens of farmers used power-tools to strip the trees as fast as they could â one eye on the ridge above us, where a group of settlers at a new illegal outpost had already gathered, and were watching the olive harvest below. Standing on ladders, the Palestinian farmers worked quickly, sending streams of olives onto the plastic sheets laid out under the trees. Three villages had come together to harvest these olives, the landowner Amin Khalil, told me, as a form of protection against attack. He said his land was now surrounded by seven Jewish settlements and outposts. Image caption, Yaser AlKam was left bloodied from the attack All Israeli settlements are illegal under international law. Outposts â small encampments on hilltops â are illegal under Israeli law as well, but many still receive state support. "This is a hotspot â there are seven settlements around here," Amin Khalil told me. "This year, all the people came together because when there are just a few people working alone at the edge of the village, the settlers attack. So all the families are working together today." But the tactic doesn't work today. As we watch, dozens of settlers, all dressed in black, begin moving down the hill towards us, setting fire to several groups of olive trees. There are shouts of panic from the Palestinian farmers, yelling for children to get out of the field. Some begin swiftly wrapping up the olives to leave. But with large numbers of people on both sides, the confrontation stalls into an uneasy stalemate. We see settlers with slingshots hurl stones towards us, and young Palestinian men running to throw stones in return. As Israeli forces arrive, the standoff explodes into action. Settlers begin running down towards us as the farmers swiftly retreat. Some Palestinians set off fireworks to try and push the settlers back. Image source, Reuters Image caption, The UN says settler attacks this year have so far killed one Palestinian and injured more than 120 others American journalist Heidi Levine of the Washington Post was injured in the attack. She described how dozens of settlers ambushed her as she was reporting at the scene. "I got jumped," she said. "I was on the ground and they were kicking me and I was trying to hold onto my camera and my bag. I had my helmet and flak jacket on which protected me. They made me stand up and they kicked me again, and this went on for at least 10 minutes." In a statement, Washington Post executive editor Matt Murray said Levine had been clearly identifiable as a journalist. "We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities," he said. Despite the video evidence and testimony, the Israeli prime minister's office said the facts remained unclear and were under investigation. The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said personnel had been despatched to the area "following a report of a violent confrontation". It said a female journalist had been injured during the confrontation. And that "all circumstances" surrounding the incident would be examined. As the farmers retreated, the sound of live ammunition cracked across the fields. It was unclear if settlers or Israeli forces were firing. Minutes later, Israeli forces began firing tear gas into the Palestinian fields to end the confrontation â a well-worn Israeli pattern of managing these conflicts. The UN says settler attacks on the olive harvest this year have so far killed one Palestinian and injured more than 120 others across the West Bank. Illegal Jewish outposts have mushroomed here over the past few years, clustering in closer around Palestinian olive groves. What we witnessed was part of a pattern being repeated day after day, as settler outposts here increase. The yearly olive harvest has become a litmus test of how the policies of Israel's fiercely pro-settlement government are affecting Palestinians here, by presiding over growing violence by extremist settlers, and fuelling Jewish claims to the land. title: Patients in chains rescued from suspected illegal rehab centre in South Africa
page_title: Mpumalanga rehab centre: South African police rescue 200 people, some in chains - BBC News
summary: Some of the 200 patients were found with "sores all over their bodies" and in overcrowded rooms.
text: Image source, Department of social development Image caption, Officials uncovered "gross inhuman conditions" when they raided the centre By Khanyisile Ngcobo Reporting from Johannesburg Published 16 October 2026, 14:09 BST Updated 5 hours ago A pastor and his wife have been arrested in South Africa after 200 people, some in chains, were found held at a suspected illegal rehabilitation centre in the north-eastern part of the country. The facility, operated from a church in Mpumalanga province, was discovered during an operation by officials in the area on Thursday. Authorities said they uncovered "gross inhumane conditions" when they raided the facility, with some patients found with "sores all over their bodies" and "others chained to each other". Police have since charged the couple, who were running the facility, with kidnapping but could add more charges. They have not yet commented. Illegal rehabilitation centres have mushroomed in South Africa in recent years as drug use spirals in the country. Last year, the department of social development said it had uncovered over 100 unlawful facilities operating across the country, mostly in Gauteng province, home to the country's largest city, Johannesburg. A girl of 16 and a boy of 11 were found being kept in the same room as adults in the Mpumalanga centre. Image source, South Africa Police Service Image caption, Two minors were among the 200 people found living in crowded rooms at the facility The couple running it told officials they were housing 60 people, but upon inspection, more than three times that number were found, including more than 30 women. The group, mostly believed to be drug addicts, were found in crowded rooms and without access to functioning bathrooms or running water. "Some [of them had] been at the alleged illegal centre for a while," the department said. Gift Skhosana, one of those held at the facility, told local broadcaster Newzroom Afrika it was "common practice" for patients to be chained. "They chain us as punishment [and] when you gain entry," he said. Despite this, Skhosana, who was a drug user, said the facility helped him get clean and overcome his addiction. Another person, who was not named, said his experience with the facility left him needing help mentally. The couple charged a monthly fee of 3,000 rand ($182; Â£137) to house the patients, of which almost a half would go to the church. Fourteen of those found at the centre have since been taken to hospital for further medical treatment, police said. Officials said 132 have been reunited with their families. The couple is expected to appear in a local court on Monday. title: Pope pictured for first time since surgery and cancer diagnosis
page_title: Pope pictured for first time since surgery and cancer diagnosis - BBC News
summary: The pontiff was diagnosed with lung cancer after having surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday.
text: Image source, Vatican via Reuters Image caption, Pope Leo thanked medical staff as he was pictured for the first time since his lung surgery By Henry Moore Published 6 hours ago Pope Leo XIV has been pictured celebrating Mass from hospital, in the first images of him released by the Vatican since he underwent lung surgery. The 71-year-old pontiff was diagnosed with lung cancer after the surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday afternoon, which the Vatican said had been "successful" and proceeded without complications. The images shared on Friday showed the Chicago-born Pope wearing a green robe while standing behind a makeshift altar on the tenth floor of the hospital. Pope Leo "celebrated with the medical and nursing staff" and thanked workers for their service, the Vatican press office said. Pope's cancer diagnosis leaves Catholics questioning what comes next Published 2 days ago On Friday, the Pope's doctors said tests had shown "a steady improvement in his general condition" since his procedure. His doctors said that a chest X-ray indicated "good recovery of the operated lung". The whole lower lobe of the Pope's right lung was removed "to ensure the procedure was radical", the Vatican said following the surgery. "After the operation, the Pope awoke normally and returned after a brief period of observation to his room," it said earlier, before he spent a "peaceful night" at the hospital. Image source, Vatican via Reuters Image caption, The pontiff is expected to remain at the hospital for about a week as he recovers Pope Leo first announced that he would be having the operation during his weekly Sunday prayers, telling the crowd in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a "well-contained" nodule on his lung "at an early stage" and advised him to have it removed. Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous, but after it was examined the medical team confirmed it was, "as suspected by pre-operative tests", the Vatican said. He was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma. The Vatican has stressed that the Pope had shown no symptoms of infection or illness prior to the procedure. title: Russia accuses Ukraine of attacking oil refinery after Zelensky says strikes to resume
page_title: Russia accuses Ukraine of attacking oil refinery after Zelensky says strikes to resume - BBC News
summary: Ukraine's president says a pause on striking energy sites is over following fresh Russian attacks.
text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Ukraine's President Zelensky accused the US of withdrawing intelligence-sharing about Russian strikes to place pressure on Kyiv By Maia Davies Â and Â Sarah Rainsford ,Â Southern and Eastern Europe correspondent Published 15 October 2026 Russia has accused Ukraine of attacking an oil refinery on Thursday after President Volodymyr Zelensky said such strikes, halted at the request of the US, would resume. Zelensky said he had restricted attacks for three days while Russia continued striking Ukraine's energy infrastructure. "We're done," he told the Financial Times , external . Russian President Vladimir Putin said Kyiv had also tried to hit refineries on Wednesday - which Ukraine denied - but there had been no "significant damage". Zelensky also accused the US of withdrawing intelligence-sharing to pressure Kyiv into ending attacks but Ukrainian defence sources later told the BBC some functionality on Starlink satellite services had resumed. They said "operation while on the move", part of Starlink's military service Starshield, had been restored, although it remains unclear whether restrictions on the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining Starlink internet connection have been fully lifted. Officials were still working to clarify "the reasons and circumstances" behind the move, the sources added. In a separate development, seven people are missing after a drone attack set a chemical tanker on fire off Romania , according to naval officials. Moscow said it had hit two cargo ships with military cargo heading to Ukraine's Odesa port, without naming them. Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine? Published 1 day ago Eight crew missing after drone attack leaves tanker ablaze off Romania's coast Published 1 day ago The Kremlin said Kyiv had "attempted a large-scale attack" on a refinery south of Moscow early on Thursday. According to Russia's defence ministry, four missiles and dozens of drones were intercepted and the falling debris caused a fire at the site in Ryazan. Zelensky said dozens of Ukrainian cities had come under Russian attack in the past day. He previously said he would agree to the "energy ceasefire" announced by US President Donald Trump on Sunday if Moscow also abided by it. But he accused Russia of ignoring the proposed deal within hours of it being announced, with strikes leaving hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians without power. The Kremlin never said it had agreed to the deal. Zelensky agreed that he felt betrayed by the US when asked by Piers Morgan on Wednesday night, after Washington appeared to withdraw key elements of its support. European leaders have rallied around the Ukrainian president. Italy's Defence Minister Guido Crosetto told the BBC that the US restricting its intelligence-sharing with Kyiv would be a "complete mistake". "Because it is a fundamental form of support. This means denying a country any chance of defending itself." He added: "Peace will be achieved when Putin will be convinced that there is a stalemate... that he cannot advance anymore. But if he sees a weakness on the Ukrainian front, if the United States takes its resources away, then Putin will think he can win, and so he will continue the war." Zelensky met Nato chief Mark Rutte as a two-day summit of European leaders began in Brussels on Thursday. The head of the military alliance said they had discussed "the importance of implementing an energy ceasefire as well as Nato allies' continuous support for Ukraine". Zelensky told the FT that Ukrainian officials had been told by US counterparts that "if you will not stop [the strikes], we will block intelligence". Ukraine's military relies on US early-warning alerts of incoming Russian aerial attacks to mount air defences, limiting successful strikes, while Starlink internet links are used throughout its war effort to guide drones and protect its skies. There were suggestions a technical glitch was to blame for the sudden Starlink restrictions on Tuesday evening, but owner Elon Musk appeared to deny this and suggested it was the Trump administration's doing . "It was not a technical problem, it was the will," Zelensky told the FT. Trump has denied halting intelligence-sharing. Starlink's sister service Starshield is provided to Ukraine under a US defence department contract. The BBC has approached the US authorities for comment. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Zelensky has questioned Trump's relationship with Russia President, Vladimir Putin Zelensky spoke to the FT during a visit to London on Wednesday which also included a meeting with Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Downing Street - who announced the UK would speed up delivery of lightweight multirole missiles to Kyiv . The Ukrainian president told the newspaper he would now only halt strikes on Russian oil infrastructure - which Kyiv says are vital to cutting off revenue streams to its war machine - if the US supplied more Patriot air defence missiles. Ukraine has suffered a shortage of the US-made defences since the outbreak of the Iran war consumed stockpiles. Striking a more defiant tone than recently, the Ukrainian president told the newspaper his American counterpart had an affinity for autocratic leaders like Putin. He said it was not up to him to mend US-Ukrainian relations given the events of the past week: "We didn't destroy any relationship." Tensions have previously frayed between the two leaders. After returning to the White House last year, the pair shared a fiery Oval Office meeting in which Trump implied Zelensky was the main block to a peace deal. Zelensky has since walked a careful diplomatic line, showing willingness towards US-brokered deals while stressing that the terms of any peace deal must be just. But he criticised the agreement between Russia and the US to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US and global marketplace , struck last week, as the US effectively investing in Russia's war effort. Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images Image caption, Two people were killed in Sloviansk, Donetsk, after overnight strikes, where a number of residential buildings were destroyed That deal was the latest effort by Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war, which has sent fuel costs skyrocketing. Zelensky told the FT: "The question will be: when will the next deal be? Maybe it will be gas. Definitely it will be gas." With Russia continuing to strike Ukraine, Zelensky suggested the disruptions to US support was no coincidence. Local officials report at least 13 people were killed across Ukraine on Wednesday in what Zelensky called a "constant", large-scale Russian attack. He said more than 850 drones had been launched at dozens of cities and communities. At least three people were killed in the central region of Kirovohrad as it suffered its largest attack since Russia's full-scale invasion began in 2022, officials there said, with nearly 360 drones launched during a 10-hour barrage. Deaths were also reported in Donetsk, Kherson and Volyn. "It is clear that Russia deliberately escalated these attacks, taking advantage of the easing of sanctions and seeing attempts to pressure Ukraine," Zelensky wrote on social media. title: School headscarf ban sparks rare protests in Azerbaijan and row with Turkey
page_title: School headscarf ban sparks rare protests in Azerbaijan and row with Turkey - BBC News
summary: Protests have taken place over the rules which have seen pupils wearing hijabs turned away from schools.
text: Image source, Azerbaijani social media Image caption, These schoolgirls were not allowed to enter classes because of their headscarves By Rayhan Demytrie Caucasus correspondent Published 15 October 2026 "You are telling me, I can't come to school?" says a teenage girl in a navy blue Islamic headscarf, captured on video challenging a staff member at the entrance to her school. The footage has been shared widely on social media, and shows a group of girls in hijabs standing behind her applauding as she continues: "Why should I have to give up my religion?" Last Monday the education ministry in Azerbaijan began enforcing new uniform rules, turning away female pupils wearing hijabs. Protests began outside state schools in the capital, Baku, and in several southern districts including Masally and Jalilabad. Protests are rare in this oil- and gas-producing country of 10.5 million people. Azerbaijan is constitutionally secular and the government strongly enforces that. President Ilham Aliyev has been in power since 2003 and has little tolerance for dissent. Opposition politicians and many independent journalists are in jail. Azerbaijan is pulled between two neighbours, Turkey and Iran. Azerbaijanis belong to a Turkic group of nations, speaking a language close to Turkish, and Turkey is its closest ally. But like Iran to the south, Azerbaijan is mainly Shia - over 60% of its people identify as Shia Muslims, while most Turks are Sunni. The interior ministry said it had detained 37 people on Monday who tried to obstruct the rules and "grossly violate public order". Image source, Social media Image caption, Videos have circulated of protests taking place in and around the capital Baku The rules, approved on 21 September, ban clothing which contradict "the principle of secularism in education" in state schools. They do not mention the hijab. Similar guidelines were extended to teachers on 6 October. In one video, pupils outside School No. 69 in Balakhany, outside Baku, hold a banner reading: "The hijab does not prevent anyone from getting an education." Shahiza Huseynova, a mother who was protesting outside a school in the Mashtaga district of the capital, was detained on Tuesday. In an interview with Meydan TV, an independent Azerbaijani-language channel based in Germany, Huseynova's husband Agha said she had been given a warning: "Either you take off your child's hijab and send them to school, or you go to prison." Image source, Azerbaijan education ministry Image caption, An example shared by the Azerbaijani government of an acceptable school uniform under the new rules Friends have also lost contact with Ilkin Huseynov, an activist who on Tuesday launched an online platform called "Let Leyli Go to School". It offers free lessons from volunteer teachers to pupils barred from class. According to a friend, Huseynov left his home in Baku with unidentified men at about 16:00 on Wednesday, and his phone has been switched off ever since. The authorities have not commented, but friends believe he has been detained. On Thursday, the platform's Instagram page could not be accessed. Since the protests began, users have reported problems accessing Instagram and TikTok without a virtual private network (VPN). Most of the protests have been in religiously conservative neighbourhoods in Baku's outlying settlements and in southern districts near the 765km (475-mile) border with Iran. The authorities have long been wary of religious influence from Iran, where more ethnic Azerbaijanis live than in Azerbaijan itself. On the night of 13 October, Azerbaijan's State Service for Special Communications and Information Security said a "foreign hacker group" had attacked more than 100 state websites. A pro-Iranian group calling itself the 313 Team (Cyber Islamic Resistance) claimed responsibility. Azerbaijani officials have defended the rules. One MP, Nigar Arpadarai, told the 1news.az website that children did not choose to wear the hijab themselves but were influenced by their families. "A child has no freedom to choose a religion. This is a conscious prerogative of adults," she said. Azerbaijan pardons Frenchman after EU lifts sanctions on Russian billionaire Published 23 September Azerbaijan and Armenia sign peace pledge at White House summit with Trump Published 9 August 2025 The row has now spilled over into Turkey, Baku's closest ally, which provided vital support during Azerbaijan's 2020 war with Armenia over Nagorno-Karabakh. The two countries call themselves "one nation, two states". President Recep Tayyip ErdoÄan, a devout Muslim, has spoken of creating a "pious generation". His chief adviser, Oktay Saral, has called the Azerbaijani restrictions "unacceptable" and urged Baku to "reverse this mistake". "A headscarf is not an obstacle; it is a requirement of one's faith!" Saral wrote on X. Several MPs from Turkey's governing AK Party joined in. Small demonstrations were held outside Azerbaijan's embassy in Ankara, organised by KÃ¶klÃ¼ DeÄiÅim, an Islamist movement linked to Hizb ut-Tahrir, and outside its consulate in Istanbul, organised by conservative Islamist group ÃzgÃ¼r-Der. President Aliyev's New Azerbaijan Party accused Turkish officials of an "openly defamatory" information campaign and of "baseless accusations", warning that Oktay Saral's comments risked harming ties, and cautioned against interference in Azerbaijan's internal affairs. Earlier this month, Ilham Aliyev himself said no one should "stick their noses into our way of life". Behind the dispute there may lie another source of friction. Turkish protesters have linked the headscarf rules to Azerbaijan's close ties with Israel, which sells weapons to Baku and buys Azerbaijani oil. Turkey's relations with Israel have collapsed over Gaza, but Azerbaijan has tried to maintain relationships with both countries. That is a difficult balancing act. On Thursday, when Israel's President Isaac Herzog addressed a regional security summit hosted by Azerbaijan in Baku, delegations from Turkey, Iran and other countries walked out of the hall. title: Seven crew missing after drone attack leaves tanker ablaze off Romania's coast
page_title: Seven crew missing after drone attack leaves tanker ablaze off Romania's coast - BBC News
summary: A search and rescue operation is under way in the Black Sea after the latest attack in the area.
text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, A search and rescue operation involving boats and helicopters is now continuing in rough seas, Romania's authorities say By Jaroslav Lukiv Published 15 October 2026 Seven of 12 crew members are missing after a drone attack left a chemical tanker ablaze off Romania's coast on Thursday morning, naval authorities say. The San Marino-flagged Wine Trader was 13 nautical miles (24km) east of the mouth of the River Danube at Sulina, when it reported blasts and a fire. Romanian President NicuÈor Dan confirmed that the Wine Trader and another chemical tanker in the area, the Yara J, had both been struck by drones - the Yara J on Wednesday. The Wine Trader was empty of cargo at the time. Moscow said two cargo ships with military cargo heading to Ukraine's Odesa port had been hit. It did not name the vessels. Overnight, a swarm of Russian drones was detected not far from the scene, near Ukraine's Snake Island. The west coast of the Black Sea has recently seen a spate of drone attacks. On Tuesday, two merchant ships were struck by drones further south along the coast of Bulgaria, Romania's neighbour, and one of the vessels sank, leaving 11 crew members missing. Bulgaria said it suspected Russia was behind that attack, summoning the country's envoy. A search and rescue operation for the missing members of the Wine Trader continues, Romania's authorities have said. Two Black Hawk helicopters and two rescue boats have been deployed. The Romanian interior ministry has released a video showing one of the helicopters hovering above the vessel. The priority is now to reach the four crew members confirmed to be alive, while ensuring the safety of rescue teams with very high waves reported in the area. The Wine Trader tanker, which was sailing from Tunisia to Romania, reported several explosions on board at about 07:00 (05:00 GMT). Romanian media cited crews on nearby ships as saying the Wine Trader had been hit by two drones. The leaders of Romania and Bulgaria are due to discuss shortly whether Article 4 of the Nato treaty should be invoked. This allows any member of the military alliance to request consultations with its allies if it believes its territorial integrity or security is threatened. The Romanian president said: "We want to have all the information about what happened, but there will be a response from the Romanian state." Dan is due to meet Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte in Brussels alongside Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev to discuss growing security threats in the Black Sea region. The Romanian president said discussions would focus on operational requirements, including additional equipment to protect shipping in the area. Ukraine has directly blamed Russia for earlier attacks on civilian vessels in the western side of the Black Sea - a key route for Ukrainian exports and imports. On Tuesday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen spoke of the Black Sea becoming "another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine. This is unacceptable". Russia's military has recently intensified its strikes on vessels in the area, as part of its war against Ukraine. A fire broke out on the Comoros-flagged Yara J late on Wednesday after being struck by a drone, but its crew - who are all reportedly safe - were able to douse the flames themselves. Last week, another two ships were struck off Bulgaria, and on the same day Ukraine hit an oil tanker in the Russian Black Sea port of Sochi. Moscow says it is targeting ships delivering weapons and dual-use cargo to Ukrainian ports. Kyiv and its European allies say merchant vessels carrying grain and other civilian cargo are being attacked. Both Russia and Ukraine are major grain-exporting countries and Turkey has called on both countries to halt attacks in the Black Sea. Moscow has repeatedly rejected calls by the US and Europe for a naval ceasefire in the Black Sea, blaming Ukraine for attacking Russian merchant ships in the area. Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory . Related topics War in Ukraine Romania Russia Bulgaria Drones Europe

title: Ship attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports slow
page_title: Ship attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports slow - BBC News
summary: BBC Verify analysis of data from a UK maritime agency shows 12 vessels were struck in a week.
text: By Joshua Cheetham ,Â Thomas Copeland Â and Â Alison Benjamin ,Â BBC Verify Published 16 October 2026, 06:00 BST The number of ships that have reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz has hit a record high, BBC Verify analysis of data from a UK maritime agency shows. Twelve vessels were attacked between 5 and 11 October - the largest number of weekly strikes reported to the UK's Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency since the US-Israeli war with Iran began. The previous week saw 10 ships reporting attacks. Six of the vessels were struck last Sunday, according to the UKMTO - a one-day high. So far this week, there have been four reported attacks. As the number of strikes has risen, the recovery in oil shipments through the strait seen last month has slowed, industry data suggests. BBC Verify collated incident reports published by the UKMTO on its website and created a timeline based on the first date cited in each report. This is approximate because some incidents use the date of the attack and some the date on which it was reported. Experts say Tehran has been attacking ships in an effort to assert greater control over the waterway as the US military has increased the number of tankers it is shepherding through the south of the strait to evade Iranian strikes. Iran is also carrying out more attacks on vessels further away from the Strait of Hormuz, according to experts. The US military's Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, posted on social media that despite the attacks "commercial traffic continues to flow through the Strait of Hormuz with co-ordinated protection from US forces and regional partners". Two crew missing after one of Sunday's attacks The aftermath of one of Sunday's six reported attacks was captured in verified footage showing the Nicaragua-flagged tanker Petro Dolphin on fire, as filmed by the crew on a smaller boat nearby. The vessel was struck by a drone close to the Sohar Anchorage, Oman, more than 250km (150 miles) from the strait, according to the maritime intelligence firm Vanguard. Eleven Indian seafarers were rescued but two are still missing, the Forward Seamen's Union of India said. Attacks have continued this week with the container ship GFS Pride sinking after a strike by an unknown projectile in the strait on Tuesday. Twenty-one crew were safely evacuated. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) published footage of what appeared to be the same ship sinking. It said the vessel was carrying "2,500 containers of contraband" and had taken an "unauthorised route". Oil shipments stall Middle East oil exports have slowed as the number of ship strikes has risen. About 12.6 million barrels per day went through the strait on 13 October, below the 15 million reported at the end of September, data from trade intelligence firm Kpler shows. This compares with a pre-war baseline of some 17 million barrels per day. The recent increase in attacks comes as US Navy data indicates the number of vessels given assistance to navigate the Strait of Hormuz during the first 10 days of October was up 85% compared with the same period in August. Most of the oil being shipped from Gulf Arab states recently has been carried using a "shuttle" system where a fleet of tankers load up and sail through the strait before transferring their cargo to larger tankers in the Gulf of Oman. These shuttle ships use a route close to Oman's coastline. Iran says this is "unauthorised" and insist vessels take an alternative route closer to its own shore. So-called assisted transits were a key factor in helping drive oil flows from the Middle East back towards pre-war levels in September. This does not include Iranian exports which have completely stalled as a result of the US blockade of Iranian ports and ships. Martin Kelly, CEO of Orbital Risk Intelligence, said Iran has "evolved its strategy" in response to this loosening of its control over the strait and has been carrying out "near daily or multiple attacks every single day". "The aim here is to stop the ships going through and to deter others," he added. The IRGC's navy has said strikes would not be "limited to the Strait of Hormuz" and later announced a "new deployment formation" across the region, according to state media. Martin Kelly told BBC Verify that Iran is widening its attacks and targeting ships near the coast of Gulf Arab states and in the Gulf of Oman. A tanker was struck by multiple projectiles north of Qatar on Thursday 8 October, more than 500km (310 miles) from the strait, resulting in multiple reported casualties, according to Vanguard. Another tanker was attacked close to the UAE town of Al-Jazirah al-Hamra on Friday 9 October, Vanguard said. Verified footage shows crew members running across the deck and putting on lifejackets as a large cloud of black smoke rises over the ship. Additional reporting by Becky Dale Graphics by Tom Shiel and Mark Edwards Related topics Iran war Iran

title: They fled Russia, but the West sent them back
page_title: They fled Russia, but the West sent them back - BBC News
summary: Over the past year there has been a stark rise in anti-government activists deported to Russia from the EU and US where they were seeking refuge.
text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Criticising the government, whether on the street or on social media, can result in a prison sentence in Russia (file pic) By Will Vernon Published 16 October 2026, 05:57 BST Russian security services were waiting when the flight landed in Moscow in December. On board were Russians the US had deported, including activists denied political asylum. "It was unbelievably frightening. My knees were shaking with fear," says Katya, one of the deportees. We have changed her name to protect her identity, as she remains in Russia. Katya had left Russia and claimed asylum in the US two years earlier. When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, many countries publicly welcomed fleeing Russians. But more than four years later, attitudes have hardened. The numbers of anti-war Russians forcibly returned from Western countries is rising, and Katya's experience highlights the potential risks they face. US authorities rejected her application for asylum, after she said she had provided evidence that she had taken part in protests and was a member of an opposition movement. In Moscow, Katya says officers from the FSB security service handed all the male deportees military papers, requiring them to register with the local enlistment office, from where men are often sent to the war in Ukraine. Another passenger on the flight and an activist confirmed her account. Image source, FSB Image caption, Russian security services frequently televise special operations against perceived "spies" and "traitors" The officers interrogated her, and many others, for several hours. "At one point, they found incriminating information on my phone," says Katya, "Their faces changed in a second. I was very afraid that they would simply bundle me off somewhere." Katya was eventually released and allowed to stay with relatives. But she says police continue to call her and visit her at home. "I feel as if I'm in a cage, like in a zoo," she says, "Whenever I see a police car, I feel terrified and start thinking, "What if they're coming for me?" Katya showed the BBC documents and photographs confirming her story, which matches accounts from other deportees. Removals from the US rose from 222 in 2023 to more than 1,200 in 2025, amid a wider increase in deportations under President Donald Trump's second term. Activists say Russian deportees included dissidents and Russian army deserters, some of whom were imprisoned or sent to war after returning to Russia. One such case is Leonid Melekhin, an anti-war activist who sought asylum in the US after being arrested at protests in Russia. He had posted photographs of Russian President Vladimir Putin online with the message "Putin: murderer, fascist, usurper". After being deported back home last year, Melekhin was charged with "justifying terrorism" and sentenced to six years in prison. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Andrei Pivovarov was imprisoned in a penal colony for four years for "carrying out activities of an undesirable organisation" "We have several examples of people who got eight years in prison when they crossed the [Russian] border," says Andrei Pivovarov, from Russia's exiled opposition Anti-War Committee. And deportations are taking place from Europe too. His organisation has changed its advice to dissidents escaping Russia: the EU is no longer safe, it is better to seek refuge elsewhere. Germany has sharply increased the number of Russian nationals it deports. Seven were sent back in 2023, rising to more than 110 in 2025, according to German government figures. More than 21,000 Russians sought asylum in Germany between 2022 and 2025, but the proportion of positive decisions fell from 29% in 2023 to just 6.8% in the first eleven months of 2025. "Protection is only granted if there is an actual, well-founded fear of persecution," Germany's migration and asylum agency, BAMF, told the BBC. Last year, Berlin suspended its humanitarian visa programme for Russians, and across the EU, the proportion of Russian applicants granted some form of asylum protection fell from 23% in 2024 to around 17% in the first nine months of 2025, according to EU data. Russian opposition activists fleeing repression have become caught up in a wider crackdown on immigration, as governments across Europe and the US toughen rules amid political pressure over high numbers of irregular migrants and asylum applications, as well as over security concerns. Western governments are "focused on limiting humanitarian programmes and asylum seekers", says lawyer Anastasia Burakova, founder of rights group Kovcheg (Ark), which helps anti-war Russians leave the country. The clampdown is "in response to public concerns and rising support for right-wing populist parties", she adds. Following a negative asylum decision, Russian nationals are often given the chance to leave independently, but a rising number are being forcibly returned to Russia, usually escorted via third countries. Several Russian activists in exile told the BBC that immigration officials had told them they faced "no danger" in Russia, and that officials often lacked an adequate understanding of the risks that activists face. "I tried to explain that if they sent me back, I would be put in prison, or sent to war where I'd be killed," explains former soldier Artyom, who deserted from the Russian Army in 2022 after officers threatened to send him to Ukraine. "They just didn't believe me." Image source, Provided by contributor Image caption, Artyom deserted the Russian army in 2022 but was deported back to Russia via Egypt He says he provided US authorities with proof that a criminal investigation had been opened against him back in Russia for desertion. But he was put on a deportation flight back to Moscow via Egypt. "I was preparing for death," says the former soldier, "I was thinking, 'how can I die without it being painful?'". Back in Moscow, Artyom was held in a military detention facility but managed to escape. He is now in hiding abroad. "Another country could investigate me better and give me asylum. Why didn't they give me that chance? Instead they deported me specifically to Russia," says the deserter. "It ruined my life." The US Department of Homeland Security told the BBC: "All illegal aliens receive due process. If a judge finds an illegal alien has no right to be in this country, we are going to remove them." The asylum clampdown comes as repression inside Russia has reached "an unprecedented level", according to Nobel Prize-winning Russian human rights group Memorial. Their list of political prisoners grew from 803 to 1,265 during 2025, a record increase. The Russian Embassy in London did not respond to a request for comment. Anti-war activist Mikhail says he and his wife Dasha are awaiting deportation from Finland "any day". Their names have been changed to protect their identity, as Mikhail fears for relatives back home. Russian authorities blocked his social media accounts over anti-war posts, and police visited his mother and accused him of spreading "fake information". Image source, Reuters Image caption, There are rumours there may be a fresh wave of mobilisation to boost ranks in Ukraine Dasha is a Jehovah's Witness, an organisation banned as "extremist" in Russia. The couple provided Finnish authorities with evidence, seen by the BBC, including a video of Russian police telling his mother that more than 300 posts had violated Russian law. A single post can result in a long prison sentence. The Finnish Immigration Service has rejected their asylum request five times, deciding there is "no reasonable basis to believe" the couple would face serious rights violations if returned. "We're sitting here and someone could knock on our door at any moment, take us to the Russian border and simply hand us over to Russian officers," says Mikhail. "We fear for our lives!" "We came to Finland for help, and they're refusing us," he adds. "My wife cries constantly." Amnesty International, which is supporting the couple, says they could face a "real risk" of detention, prosecution, imprisonment and torture if returned. The Finnish Immigration Service said all asylum decisions were based on international refugee law standards, and the share of Russian citizens receiving asylum was in line with EU averages. For Mikhail and Dasha, the threat of deportation comes as more Russians may be considering leaving. There are rumours that Vladimir Putin may announce a new wave of mobilisation to boost the ranks of his army in Ukraine, which the Kremlin denies. The last mobilisation in 2022 prompted hundreds of thousands of Russians to flee, many to ex-Soviet states such as Armenia and Georgia. Anastasia Burakova's organisation says requests for help from Russians wanting to leave rose tenfold in August compared with May. For those now looking to escape, the question is whether the West will offer them refuge â or send them back. title: Tip-off foiled US teen suspect's plot to attack Hindu temple, police say
page_title: Tip-off foiled US teen's plot to attack Hindu temple, police say - BBC News
summary: The alleged plot only failed because the 19-year-old suspect's gun jammed outside the place of worship, say police.
text: Image source, Getty Images By Caitlin Doherty BBC News Published 15 October 2026 Updated 16 October 2026 00:27 BST A Taco Bell cashier's alleged plot for a mass shooting at a Hindu temple near Chicago was thwarted by a tip-off from one of his colleagues, investigators say. Alexandros Paporakis, 19, from Palatine, Illinois, appeared in court on Wednesday charged with one count of making a terrorist threat and one count of unlawful possession of a weapon. Paporakis allegedly sent a message about the planned attack on Sunday to the co-worker, who alerted authorities, officials said. Police said they found writings in which Paporakis identified as a white supremacist and wrote about his hatred for non-white people. Palatine police chief William Nord said on Thursday they were notified about a mass shooting plot on Sunday by someone who had received "concerning electronic communications" from Paporakis. "These communications played a vital role in bringing this matter to the attention of law enforcement," said the police chief. According to CBS, the BBC's US partner, prosecutors said the tipster had worked with Paporakis. Nord said a red Honda RDX registered to Paporakis entered the car park of a "known Hindu temple" in the suburb of Aurora at Sunday lunchtime. The suspect allegedly tried to open fire, but the gun jammed, so he drove home, where he lived with his mother. According to NBC Chicago, Paporakis told his colleague over phone messages that his gun had jammed and he got out of there "super-fast". Once home, he "searched internet trying to learn how to unjam his gun & called a colleague informing them of [his] intent to carry out a mass shooting", reports NBC Chicago. He is thought to have acted alone. The police chief said officers had searched Paporakis' home, where they found a rifle, loaded magazines, hundreds of rounds of rifle ammunition and body armour. Nord said they also discovered an eight-page document by the suspect containing "extremist ideologies" and revealing his plans for an attack. In the writings, he described himself as a "sociopathic white supremacist neo-Nazi", according to CBS. Police have questioned Paporakis' mother, who was said to be unco-operative. The Hindu temple identified by local media as the intended target said it had implemented new security measures. India's Ministry of External Affairs said the incident "adds to growing concerns over racist hostility and anti-India hate in the US". US congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi of Illinois said he was "horrified" by the incident. In a Facebook statement, he said he and his family worship at the temple and were there last Sunday. The Chicago metropolitan area is home to one of the biggest Indian-American populations in the US. title: Toxic algorithms wouldn't let them go - now Australia wants an off switch
page_title: Social media algorithms: What if you could turn them off? - BBC News
summary: Australia has proposed a switch to force social media platforms to let users turn off recommended content.
text: Figure caption, Watch: Many social platforms already have following-only feeds - here's how they work By Tiffanie Turnbull Sydney Published 2 hours ago Warning: This article contains an account of living with an eating disorder Varsha Yajman was already self-conscious about the way she looked when she joined social media as a 13-year-old. Endless workout videos making impossible promises filled her feeds. Through the screen, girls she'd never met urged her to sign up to dangerous calorie challenges. Others proudly promoted their height and weight - even the number of times they had been sent to hospital - on their profiles in a form of twisted competition. Every night as she fell asleep, Varsha would watch a stranger on the internet diarising what they'd consumed that day. "I was like, 'I don't need to eat. I can just watch other people eat'," Varsha tells the BBC. "I would find that I'd be down these really deep rabbit holes... it was like no matter how hard you tried to get out, you couldn't." Now 24 and in recovery from anorexia, Varsha says she is still served weight loss content on social media - despite having every safety setting turned on, and an exhaustive list of banned words. Image source, Tiffanie Turnbull / BBC Image caption, Varsha Yajman says social media aggravated her eating disorder It is people like her the Australian government says it is trying to protect with a new suite of laws cracking down on big tech, which were introduced to parliament this week. The centrepiece of their proposed reforms: an algorithm switch which would force social media platforms to let users turn off recommended content. The idea is that you would only see posts from accounts you follow. It isn't the first government to try this, but existing algorithm controls are often transient and come with trade-offs in app functionality. Australia has set out to make its legislation tighter to stop this. And it hopes its new laws â which would also impose a legal duty of care on online services â will help Australians become happier and healthier. But critics are concerned Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's government has bitten off more than it can chew in its fight with big tech, while others, including the Trump administration, say the reforms threaten free speech. The choice Flynn Martin knows what it is like to be sucked into an algorithmic spiral. Self-proclaimed misogynist influencer Andrew Tate and other manosphere figures started overwhelming the then-20-year-old's social media feeds about four years ago. It was a time when Flynn, who was eventually diagnosed with bipolar disorder, was insecure, frustrated with his life and struggling with his mental health. He says he fell for the rhetoric. He soon went viral in Australia for two videos: one ranting about whether it was OK to be a straight white male, and another where he criticised a date for her frozen yoghurt order. "You find yourself in like a bit of an echo chamber... It's easy to get swept up in that," he tells the BBC. "I really bought into the idea we were living in this matrix, we had this really negative system that was designed against you. And the only way to break out of it was becoming this alpha male character." The Melbournian was only pulled from the manosphere after a period of psychosis and a hospital stay. Image source, Daniel Fermer / ABC News Image caption, Flynn Martin says he's still finding a healthy balance with social media Nowadays, he finds it tough to look back at that version of himself: "While there's a bit of shame and embarrassment... I think there is a bit of empathy for that younger man." Both Flynn and Varsha know social media alone isn't to blame for the worst chapter of their lives, but say it was a key factor. Countless others have stories of being confronted by social media content they didn't seek out, and didn't want to see â and there's long been suspicions the algorithms curating these platforms are harming users. Social media firms argue the potential risks are being overstated and that they already provide users with effective safety tools. But research emerging from around the world has been sketching a different picture. Studies have found social media use triggers a similar brain response to gambling and substance addiction , external ; that algorithms â often unsolicited â serve up content which harms users' mental health , external , and that they're spreading disinformation and increasing polarisation, driving violence offline . Court cases and whistleblowers have aired claims that these companies know the dangers and are willing to overlook them as this technology lifts user engagement and their bottom line. "The result is that they promote content that is outrageous or that invokes strong emotions from people - so it might be anger or fear or desire or lust or insecurity, whatever it is, it's going to keep us scrolling," Chanel Contos tells the BBC. Image source, Cordelia Hsu / Reuters Image caption, Consent education campaigner Chanel Contos lobbied the government for change after founding the Teach Us Consent website in 2021 While studying the topic at university, the activist - who helped reform sexual consent education standards in Australia - came up with a campaign for change. "Fix Our Feeds" demanded recommended algorithms be turned off by default, and social media users be given the choice to opt into them. Contos envisaged a nostalgic return to the social media of the early 2010s â a time when a person's social media was filled with posts from friends or people they actually followed and their feeds were finite. More than 15,000 people signed her petition, and the campaign also won the backing of two former prime ministers, several MPs, influential figures, mental health advocates, and online safety experts. The government in September said it had listened to the Australians who had backed Contos's campaign, and announced a version of her proposal: forcing big tech to introduce an algorithm switch - but stopping short of requiring it be automatically set to off. "This is not about giving government control, it is about giving people control," Albanese said. "If people want to doom scrollâ¦ that's fine, that's up to them." Meta hooked children on Facebook and Instagram, US court hears Published 18 August Social media is 'deliberately' addictive Published 4 July 2018 Image source, Hilary Wardhaugh / Getty Images Image caption, Communications Minister Anika Wells (left podium) and Australian PM Anthony Albanese (right podium) held a press conference with parents in September around the upcoming Digital Duty of Care bill The policy is part of the government's Digital Duty of Care bill, which would require online services â social media firms, gaming sites, chatbots and more â to "ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, a safe online environment". Children must be protected from "harmful" material and design features â for example, pornography and material which encourages eating disorders or harmful attitudes towards women â and adults must be protected from "seriously harmful" material and conduct, a much narrower list of illegal content. Breaches of the law could attract fines of up A$100m (Â£52m, $70m). "The digital duty of care answers a lot of the 'what abouts' of the social media minimum age law because it's much broader; it captures all online services and it shifts the onus of responsibility from the shoulders of victims onto the shoulders of the big tech operators who seek to make money off Australian users," Communications Minister Anika Wells told the BBC. The challenges There's been a muted response from big tech. Meta, Snap, TikTok, X and Google, which owns YouTube, have all declined BBC requests for comment, and have not made public statements about the legislation. In the days after the announcement, Instagram boss Adam Mosseri argued non-algorithmic feeds would mean users saw fewer posts from friends, and said he didn't believe his app was addictive â although a US jury recently ruled otherwise . "I think we conflate the way we colloquially use the word 'addicted' â like, 'I'm addicted to this show, and I'm binge-watching it' â and clinical addiction," he told a press briefing in Sydney. Image source, Jason Henry / Bloomberg via Getty Images Image caption, Instagram chief Adam Mosseri argues recommender algorithms are essential to user enjoyment Right-wing parties in Australia â and the Trump administration â have said the algorithms proposal and the broader bill both risk forcing over-moderation and censorship. But those who defend the law say that won't happen because you can still follow who you want and share what you want. "If adults listen to manosphere podcasts, or people post their views about the government, or make memes, or want to say the moon landing was fake â they can continue to do so without restriction," Wells said this week. The proposal seems to be far less divisive amongst the public and online safety experts compared with Australia's social media ban for children. However, the big question is: how will Australia implement this policy when, so far, it has been struggling to implement the ban ? Surveys suggest most children who were on social media before the ban still are, and no fines have been issued. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Australian regulators are investigating potential breaches of the social media ban The EU's attempt at introducing algorithm controls in 2023 â after which platforms rolled out following-only feeds â is a cautionary tale. Social media firms have indicated the take-up of safety and control features like this has been low and cite it as evidence users like their products the way they are. Experts say there is a reason for that. "Platforms do what the law orders, but in such a clunky way that users don't actually enjoy the option and stick with the default, algorithmic experience," researcher Chris Zomer, from the ARC Centre of Excellence for the Digital Child, wrote in The Conversation , external . On Instagram for example, when you turn off the algorithm, you can't see direct messages or access your profile and settings. When you leave the app, it reverts back to an algorithm-governed feed on your return. The only place where these issues don't exist is the Netherlands. It was changed there after a Dutch court last year found Meta in breach of the EU's Digital Services Act. Image source, Benjamin Fanjoy / Bloomberg via Getty Images Image caption, Meta lost an appeal against the Dutch court's ruling in March, meaning users in the Netherlands retain choice over their home feeds The rules for Australia aren't set in stone yet, but the government says following-only feeds must not be harder to use or less functional, that algorithm settings must be "obvious", and that they must not change without an "explicit choice" by the user, even if they leave the app. Buoyed by her success in Australia, Contos is now taking her campaign global. "We feel like Canada, UK, Australia are all very aligned on online safety... Then if those three jurisdictions are doing it, it could become a critical mass thing." Though experiences like theirs helped inspire these reforms, both Flynn and Varsha are somewhat sceptical of them. Varsha says she struggles to believe a country like Australia can outmuscle big tech: so she's not sure the Digital Duty of Care bill will work. And Flynn says lawmakers should be "realistic" about the potential of the algorithm switch: "At the end of the day we use social media as a form of entertainment." Polling earlier this month indicated two-thirds of their fellow Gen-Zs would keep their social media algorithms â though nearly half of Australians more generally would turn theirs off. Though Varsha admits she is unlikely to make much use of an algorithm switch, she appreciates having the choice. "On a bad day I'm still susceptible to all of the things that I was at 17. To know that, if I'm having a bad day, I can opt out makes me feel really good." If you've been affected by the issues raised in this story, you could speak to a health professional or an organisation that offers support. Details of organisations offering advice and support for people in the UK are available from BBC Action Line . Related topics Australia Social media regulation debate Social media Eating disorders

title: Trump calls off livestream of Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad
page_title: Trump calls off livestream of Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad - BBC News
summary: Trump said some would "rather not watch" the killing of Nidal Hasan, the first military execution in over 60 years.
text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Thirteen unarmed US military personnel were killed in a shooting rampage at Fort Hood in Texas By Nardine Saad ,Â Madeline Halpert Â and Â Ione Wells ,Â North America Correspondent Published 15 October 2026 US President Donald Trump has called off plans to livestream the execution of former US army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan by firing squad. Trump had previously said he approved of showing the death of the Fort Hood attacker, while Vice-President JD Vance cast doubt on whether it would happen and said he would not watch it. Trump's decision to cancel the livestream came after widespread criticism in the US and globally. On Thursday, he said that "many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die". "I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan," Trump said. "He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," the president added in the post on Truth Social. Hasan fatally shot 13 unarmed US military personnel and injured 32 others at a military base in Texas in 2009. His execution by firing squad will be the first military execution in more than 60 years. Trump said the families of the victims can still view the execution in person if they wish. "They deserve to witness JUSTICE!" he said. After the Pentagon announced last week that it would execute Hasan on 3 December 2026 by firing squad and livestream the event, a cascade of criticism quickly followed from human rights groups and many others. The United Nations called the plans "abhorrent". While there were more than 2,700 executions across 17 countries last year, only two nations carried them out publicly. According to Amnesty International, 11 public executions were known to have been carried out in Iran in 2025 and another six in Afghanistan. US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth defended his decision to air Hasan's execution online, saying that "people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things". Figure caption, 'We'll make sure people can watch Hasan execution' - Hegseth But as criticism mounted, Trump appeared to hedge his support, saying on Friday that he "absolutely" approved of the livestream plan, but adding that the Pentagon was still "making a determination" on it. The president also called Hasan "totally nuts". "I really don't care how he goes, as long as he goes, and I think that the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him," he said. After Trump announced he called it off, a Pentagon spokesman said Hegseth had spoken with the US president beforehand. "The Secretary supports the President's decision, and they are completely aligned," the spokesman Sean Parnell said. John Galligan, a lawyer for Hasan working primarily on civil issues, told the BBC that Trump's decision to cancel the livestream of his execution "comes as no surprise". "It was initially a dumb decision and statement by Hegseth to livestream any execution - and it violated the Army's own regulation," Galligan said. He said Hasan is paralysed from the chest down, something that Trump "allegedly didn't even know" when he approved the livestream plan. "The damage has already been done - the Army is now just trying to clean up the mess," Galligan said. "It will permanently remain a stain on our military justice system." He added that it was not clear if Hasan was aware yet of Trump's "reversal" of the livestream decision. Hasan opened fire in a crowded medical building where deploying soldiers were awaiting check-ups and vaccines. Image source, Reuters He later admitted in court that he was the gunman and apologised for "any mistakes". He said during his court martial in 2013 that he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan from the US military. The killings on 5 November 2009 were the deadliest ever non-combat attack on an American military base. US military law requires that a military execution be approved by the US president. It also requires appellate review, when a higher court inspects the decision and gives a final judgement on its legality to move forward. title: Trump denies limiting Ukraine access to Starlink network
page_title: Trump denies limiting Ukraine access to Starlink network - BBC News
summary: Speed curbs limited Ukraine's defences against deadly Russian attacks on Tuesday night.
text: Image source, Getty Images By Hafsa Khalil Published 1 hour ago US President Donald Trump has denied limiting Ukraine's access to Starlink's sister internet network Starshield after it restricted drone speed, hampering Kyiv's ability to protect itself from Russian attacks. "It wasn't me and I don't think it was [Starlink owner] Elon [Musk]," Trump said, hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said speed had yet to be restored. Musk himself suggested the US government might have been behind the restrictions, while Reuters news agency reported on Thursday that the order had come from inside the White House. Ukraine was hit by several deadly strikes on Tuesday after the network slowdown. Starlink is a civilian-use high-speed internet network operated by Musk's SpaceX. Starshield - which relies on Starlink- is its military-grade sister service that was designed for the Pentagon. The US had previously warned it could withhold sharing intelligence, crucial for Kyiv's defences, if Ukraine did not stop hitting Russian oil refineries. Tension has been brewing between Washington and Kyiv for days over a recent controversial diesel deal between Russia and the US. Zelensky - angered by the deal - resumed targeting Russian oil refineries this week in a move criticised by Trump three days after he announced a ceasefire on energy infrastructure. Kyiv said it would stop the strikes if Russia did the same but Moscow never confirmed the ceasefire and continued its attacks. "If I don't stand up to this... who else will?" Zelensky asked EU leaders at a summit on Friday. Trump had also said that Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with than [Russian President Vladimir] Putin". But speaking to reporters as he left the White House on Friday, the US president said he had a good relationship with his Ukrainian counterpart. Asked about Starshield, he said he was "not sure" it "ever came down". Musk earlier explained that Starshield was managed by the US government, and that the Pentagon could have been responsible. In its report about the alleged order regarding Starshield, Reuters quoted two US officials and a Western official briefed on the matter. The US government has allowed Ukraine to use Starlink and Starshield in its defence against Russia. Musk cut Moscow's access to the service in February, giving Kyiv an advantage in the conflict. On Tuesday night, Starlink restricted speed limits to 100mph (160km/h), meaning any weapons that travelled faster than that lost connectivity to the network. Some 600,000 in Ukraine were left without power as communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military were also hit in the deadly attacks. A bipartisan group of US senators has signed a letter demanding an investigation into the disruptions to the network. "Restrictions reportedly degraded Ukraine's ability to conduct defensive operations against Russian drone and missile attacks on civilian infrastructure," the letter read. On Friday, French President Emmanuel Macron vowed that EU states would not abandon Ukraine. Speaking at the end of the two-day summit in Brussels attended by Zelensky, Macron said it was Europe's job to hold the line in the face of some people's "ambiguities". That was apparently a reference to signs of wavering US support for Ukraine. Funding for Ukraine and helping it get through another freezing winter - its fifth since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 - topped the summit's agenda. The war will cost â¬155bn (Â£131bn; $174bn) next year, Zelensky told the European Council, with at least â¬70bn needed to come from the EU for defence and weapons. Macron said Europe was working to help Ukraine with its satellite and early warning systems, and Ukraine's friends would look at its request for further aid. title: Two dead in Istanbul after heaviest rainfall in 84 years, governor says
page_title: Two dead in Istanbul after heaviest rainfall in 84 years, governor says - BBC News
summary: Residents have been told to avoid leaving their homes unless absolutely necessary.
text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Flooding in the Kucukcekmece district of Istanbul By Emer Moreau Published 15 October 2026 Two people have died after severe flooding caused by what the governor of Istanbul said was the heaviest rainfall in 84 years, BBC Turkish has reported. A14-year-old boy died after he was electrocuted when he stepped in a puddle, while a 34-year-old man attempting to cross the road slipped and fell, hitting his head on the pavement. Nearly 600 people have been rescued after becoming stranded, the city's deputy mayor said, with cars submerged in water in some districts. Residents have been told by Istanbul Governor Davut GÃ¼l to avoid leaving their homes unless absolutely necessary. The city's governorship is investigating the death of the teenaged boy who was electrocuted. Some areas of Istanbul have seen rainfall equivalent to one seventh of the annual average, according to the interior minister. Schools were ordered to close on Thursday and Friday, as the rain is expected to continue. Nuri Aslan, deputy mayor of the city, said 595 people had been evacuated to safe areas after becoming trapped, while more than 8,000 workers were responding to the flooding. "I urge all our citizens to remain vigilant against the expected heavy rain and storm, particularly during nighttime hours," he wrote on X. He told people to use public transport instead of private vehicles, with the city's metro hours expanded to 02:00 local time. The flooding also impacted air travel, with 46 planes unable to land at airports in Istanbul, BBC Turkish said. A car park in a shopping centre was flooded in the Sariyer district, with multiple vehicles submerged. Sections of roads in other areas collapsed, according to local media, and a river has burst its banks. More than 16 million people live in the broader Istanbul metropolitan area. The interior ministry has also warned of sudden flooding in several provinces. In response, employees who are disabled, pregnant or veterans will be granted administrative leave on Thursday, unless they work in health, safety, and rainwater drainage fields, Turkish media reported. Women working in the public sector who have children under the age of eight will also be granted leave. title: I Am Artemis: Allison Mjoen
summary: As the supercooled propellant flowed into the core stage, and NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket roared to life, Allison Mjoen and her family watched with awe and pride.
